5seu76.text: The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts and an IT contractor said systems underpinning the federal bankruptcy courts are back online after a cyberattack two weeks ago caused outages. The system, called the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC), produces and transmits bankruptcy notices for all federal bankruptcy courts. The platform is maintained by British multinational BAE Systems, which said it has worked closely with the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts to restore the BNC. “No other systems were affected. No data was extracted. There was no breach of any PII,” a spokesperson for BAE Systems told Recorded Future News. No hackers ever took credit for the cyberattack, which was announced on October 22 and declared a “Bankruptcy Rules emergency” by federal court officials. The emergency declaration allowed bankruptcy judges to extend deadlines and issue related orders that allowed them to operate around the BNC outage. The emergency declaration lasts 90 days through January 2027 unless it is ended by court officials. “Although BNC has announced that services are beginning to resume, we anticipate that the emergency declaration will remain necessary throughout the restoration period,” the court said. “The declaration provides important flexibility to ensure that courts can address the effects of the outage and helps protect parties from potential prejudice resulting from delayed notice and related service disruptions.” As a result of the attack, the BNC’s production and distribution of bankruptcy notices for bankruptcy courts was halted. All access to the websites BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary — including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service — were offline. On Monday, federal court officials said the BNC will begin processing a backlog of data from courts dating back to October 7 and will start processing newly received court submissions. “Paper notices will be handled separately and released in prioritized waves based on production capacity and mailing readiness,” the court said. To address delays caused by the outages, all paper notices created between October 13 and Monday will carry a warning that notices were sent later than intended due to the cyberattack on the BNC. Those receiving paper letters are urged to contact their lawyers or check the website of the clerk’s office for the court on the notice for more information about any new deadlines. The attack on the BNC is one of several breaches of federal systems to occur in recent months. The Defense Department, FBI, ATF and Department of Transportation have all suffered breaches over the last three months. On Wednesday, hackers released stolen data on 41,000 employees of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). A DHS spokesperson said they are aware of the breach and are “actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected,” they told Recorded Future News. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

aazz8w.text: A massive search-hijacking campaign involving 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million reported installations redirected users' searches through tracking servers to generate advertising revenue from Bing and Yahoo. A new report by Socket's John Tuckner expands on the researcher's April 2025 discovery of 57 Chrome extensions with 6 million users, adding 264 newly identified add-ons with another 8.7 million users. "These extensions were created by a handful of organized operators all working from the same idea: quietly take over the browser's default search engine, route every query through a suspicious proxy server, and collect partner referral payments from Yahoo or Bing under a syndication partner ID," explained Tuckner. The extensions, with the full list shared at the bottom of Socket's report, pretend to be PDF converters, manual finders, safe search, and AI search tools. However, for the most part, the extensions simply redirect users' searches through a series of sites until they land on Bing or Yahoo. Although they are hosted on the Chrome Web Store, Google's official portal for Chrome add-ons, Socket says they are unlisted and don't appear in users' searches on the extension store. Instead, the extensions are promoted through shady advertisements found on websites. Tuckner explains that many of these extensions need almost no code to achieve their goal, as Chrome's built-in 'chrome_settings_overrides' setting allows them to replace the default search provider. One example analyzed in the report includes only a manifest and icons, with no background scripts, content scripts, or requested permissions. Browser-hijacking extensions like these have long blurred the line between potentially unwanted programs (PUPs) and malware, with BleepingComputer reporting on hundreds of similar extensions over the years. Risk extends beyond ad fraud The extensions currently focus on revenue generation through search referrals, passing user searches through an operator-controlled server before they reach Yahoo or Bing. However, Tuckner warns that the final destination can change at any time without updating the extension, including redirecting users to phishing sites or malicious downloads. "The search referral revenue is a profitable watering hole while the proxy operator can wait for data to accumulate and targets to surface before redirecting to malicious search results or landing pages for phishing or other malicious downloads," explains Tuckner. An example of this is the Predator Search extension, which redirected Tuckner to four different sites when performing six identical searches. "Six identical searches sent through its proxy search server ended in four different places: straight to Yahoo with partner tags (hspart=sz&hsimp=yhs-026), a landing page on searchlio.net, a hop through searchtosearch.com to a second results domain (mcftink.com) before Yahoo, and a Cloudflare non-responsive error page," Tuckner reported. "The extension never changed; the proxy chose each destination as the search came in." The largest recently active cluster of extensions is "Bing-Search," with 37 extensions and 2.2 million users, often promoted through Bidbrain ads. Another one is the "SecuryBrowse" wave, with 58 extensions and 4.9 million users, promoting security-themed add-ons like Fire Shield, Securify, and WatchTower. The researcher said most of these extensions had been removed from the Chrome Web Store when the report was published. However, new ones are constantly being added. Users should uninstall the extensions listed in Socket's report from their web browsers, run a full AV scan on their systems, and avoid downloading unnecessary tools and browser add-ons from unknown publishers. BleepingComputer has contacted Google for a comment on Socket's findings, but we have not received a response by publication. rkdzos.text: Threat actors are delivering malicious loaders and cryptocurrency miners under the guise of artificial intelligence (AI) desktop applications for Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT as part of a campaign dubbed Yoba. The activity involves creating fake GitHub projects that claim to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus, only to deliver a malware family called YobaLoader. "The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections," Check Point Research said in an analysis. To add to the project's credibility, the attackers set up GitHub.io pages to describe the capabilities of the software. Although the GitHub projects' popularity is not manipulated using techniques like ghost networks, signs point to the use of SEO poisoning tactics to ensure that links to them are surfaced on top of search results on Google. Some of the identified GitHub pages links are below - github[.]com/gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop gpt-5-6.github[.]io github[.]com/gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io github[.]com/gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io gpt-6-astra[.]github[.]io github[.]com/opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github[.]io opus-5-0[.]github[.]io "Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively," Check Point said. "This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor's true operational time zone." Hosted within these repositories are ZIP archives that, among other files, contain two specific components - Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI Codex or Claude executable winmm.dll, a malicious DLL that's sideloaded by the executable The DLL is a dropper codenamed YobaDropper, which implements checksum value checks by hashing the basename of its host executable and if it matches a hard-coded value "0xE6C2F326." In other words, the check requires it to be launched under "Setup.exe," and fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandboxed environment. Additional anti-analysis techniques and pre-checks include 200,000 iterations of "Sleep(5500)," which amounts to 12.73 days, and skipping machines whose keyboard layout corresponds to that of Russia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. Another language ID excluded from the infection process is Tatar. Notably missing from the list is Ukraine, which used to be historically included in such checks. YobaDropper, for its part, triggers a DLL sideloading chain of its own comprising "wmpdmc.exe" and "ampdui.dll," copying the former from its "system32" folder and placing it in a new directory named "WMProcess" created under "ProgramData." The dropper then extracts and decrypts an embedded payload, and drops it into the same folder as "wmpdui.dll." It also establishes persistence by means of a scheduled task that launches the legitimate executable to load the malicious payload. The second DLL is YobaLoader. It implements the same anti-sandbox technique as YobaDropper, requiring the malware to be run only by "wmpdmc.exe" by checking the hash against a hard-coded value ("0x552751E3"). The loader is responsible for three main tasks - Downloads an image from a Telegram channel ("t[.]me/yoba_fanclub"). Uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words and an integer value in the range 0–999 using a domain generation algorithm (DGA). The end result is domain in the format "adjective-noun-verb-digit.dedyn[.]io." Queries Google's DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain a Base64-encoded command from a DNS TXT record by passing the constructed domain as input. Decrypts the response to obtain the link to fetch the next-stage payload ("files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat"). "By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity," Check Point said. The downloaded payload is then injected into "svchost.exe," resulting in the execution of an XMRig cryptocurrency miner. Evidence indicates that the first GitHub repository was created around July 2026, although the malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August. What's more, early versions of YobaLoader have been found to only exclude Russia from infection, while also incorporating extensive anti-debugging and anti-VM checks, which have since been removed in newer versions. "The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance," Check Point said. "By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious."

yotknl.text: Microsoft has resolved a known issue that prevents non-admin users from connecting to devices via Remote Desktop when the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled. When Administrator protection is enabled, it prompts standard users to authenticate with Windows Hello (PIN or biometric) when they try to change the Windows Registry or install new apps. This feature began rolling out in October 2025 and is now enabled by default in organizations using Windows security baselines after installing the October 2026 Windows security update. Microsoft acknowledged on October 13 that Remote Desktop connections may fail with error 0xC000000D after installing the KB5124010 September 2026 non-security preview update (or Windows updates released since then) on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later. "This issue primarily affects enterprise-managed remote devices used as Remote Desktop hosts with Administrator protection enabled, regardless of how the feature was enabled," it said. Remote Desktop connection failures now fixed On Wednesday, Microsoft confirmed that this issue is fixed for users who installed this month's KB5127936 preview update. "This issue was resolved by Windows updates released October 28, 2026 (KB5127936), and later," it noted. "We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one." Microsoft also provides a temporary workaround for users who don't want to install this preview update and would rather wait for next month's Patch Tuesday cumulative updates, which requires IT administrators to disable the admin protection feature by resetting the "User Account Control Type Of Admin Approval Mode" policy via Microsoft Intune or Group Policy. Microsoft fixed a similar issue in March 2025 that was causing Remote Desktop and RDS connection failures after installing Windows updates released since January 2025. It also released emergency out-of-band Windows updates last month to fix Remote Desktop Services failures caused by the September 2026 security updates. 1ol6q65.text: Which AI agents can act inside your employees' browsers today? If an agent started browsing this morning, would you know it wasn't the employee? Most security teams can't answer those questions yet. That's not a failure of effort. It's a sign of how quickly AI moved from answering questions to taking action. AI agents now operate browsers inside authenticated applications, and they get there in different ways: debugging interfaces, extensions, agentic browsers, and emerging standards like WebMCP. Each changes what an agent can access, how its actions are attributed, and whether existing controls can see them. 1. Remote Debugging: Applications Controlling the Browser One way AI agents operate browsers isn't new at all. It's the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). CDP was built to help developers inspect, debug, and automate Chromium-based browsers. It provides programmatic access to navigation, page content, network activity, and user interactions. Tools like Playwright and Puppeteer have used it for years. AI agents use the same approach to navigate websites, extract information, fill forms, and interact with web applications. The key distinction: automation doesn't have to originate inside the browser. An external application can connect to a browser with debugging enabled and control its tabs. If that browser has authenticated sessions, the automation can use that access. To most security tools, a browser launched with debugging enabled and signed into corporate applications looks like any other authenticated browser session. The question to ask: Which applications can launch or connect to debuggable browsers? Do your policies permit this, and which corporate sessions can those applications access? 2. AI Extensions and Agentic Browsers The second approach puts the agent directly inside the browser. Extensions such as Claude in Chrome can read pages, switch tabs, click buttons, and complete multistep workflows. This requires powerful permissions, including scripting, tab access, and the debugger API. These permissions enable the functionality but also expand what the extension can access. Agentic browsers like Perplexity Comet and ChatGPT Desktop go further, building AI directly into the browsing experience. These capabilities aren't necessarily governed by extension permissions, so existing extension controls may not apply. Without an inventory of browsers across your fleet, you may not know which agents are operating. Two risks stand out. Agents act with the user's identity. When an agent downloads a document or changes an internal application setting, the application sees an authenticated user making an authorized request. Without additional telemetry, neither the application nor its audit logs may distinguish the agent's actions from the employee's. One was an employee. One was an AI agent impersonating that employee. The application logged both the same way. Agents treat content as input. A browser displays a page for someone to interpret. An agent reads that page and decides what to do next. This introduces prompt injection risks, where instructions embedded in websites, documents, or emails attempt to redirect its behavior. The result is software interpreting untrusted content while operating with trusted permissions. The question to ask: Which AI extensions and agentic browsers are running across your fleet, what access do they have, and can you distinguish their actions from an employee's? 3. WebMCP: Websites Exposing Tools Directly to Agents The third approach changes how websites interact with agents. WebMCP is an emerging web standard developed through the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group, with contributions from Google and Microsoft. Rather than interpreting pages and simulating clicks, agents can call structured tools exposed directly by websites. For example, instead of navigating a support portal and filling out forms, an agent could call a tool to create a ticket. Chrome introduced an early preview in 2026, and the specification continues to evolve. But this introduces a new trust problem. Websites aren't just presenting content. They're defining actions agents can take. Tool names, descriptions, and input schemas guide what an agent invokes. These definitions come from the website and shouldn't be treated as trusted instructions. A compromised or malicious site could use misleading descriptions or functionality to influence an agent's behavior. Site A's tool description quietly instructs the agent to pull data from Site B. Each tool operates within its website's security context, but agents working across multiple sites can move information between them. The concern isn't just what a tool does, but what data the agent provides when calling it. The question to ask: What corporate data can agents pass to website tools, where does that data go, and can you control which tools they use? What This Means for Browser Security All three approaches share one thing: software is acting on websites with the access tied to a user's browser session. That's why browser security can't assume a human is behind every click anymore. Endpoint, network, and application controls still matter. But they were built to see processes, traffic, and logins, not what an agent reads, decides, and does inside an authenticated tab. That's the gap. The goal isn't to stop employees from using AI agents. Agents are going to become a normal part of how work gets done. The goal is to make sure the controls you already expect in the browser keep applying when an agent is the one operating it. We help you discover AI-enabled browsers and extensions, monitor AI activity across your workforce, and enforce data protection policies before sensitive information leaves the tab. Want to see which agents are already operating in your environment? Request a demo with our team, and we'll walk you through it. Sponsored and written by Keep Aware.

jfq3qt.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies to patch a high-severity Linux kernel privilege escalation bug that attackers are chaining with the PHP2Shell flaws in the wild. Tracked as CVE-2026-46300 and known as Fragnesia, this vulnerability stems from a logic bug in the Linux XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that lets attackers run malicious code with root permissions. Fragnesia belongs to the Dirty Frag vulnerability class and has a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit that local attackers can use to gain root privileges on major Linux distributions with kernels released before May 13, 2026. CISA added CVE-2026-46300 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Wednesday and ordered federal agencies to patch their systems by Saturday 10, as mandated by its Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. The cybersecurity agency didn't share details about ongoing Fragnesia attacks, but it noted that threat actors could chain it with two critical PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively tracked as PHP2Shell, to deploy webshells on unpatched systems. "This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root," CISA said. Fragnesia and PHP2Shell exploit chain While CISA didn't provide more information on attackers chaining the Fragnesia and PHP2Shell flaws, Dream Security analysts said in a Monday report that the vulnerabilities were used to breach more than two dozen servers, including three belonging to a US government-affiliated organization. "Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts," they said. "This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment." CISA also added the PHP2Shell flaws to its list of actively exploited vulnerabilities on Monday and mandated that Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies secure their networks by Thursday. While the US cybersecurity agency has not yet provided further details on ongoing PHP2Shell attacks, Perplexity security engineer Adel Karimi confirmed in-the-wild exploitation over the weekend after their honeypots recorded evidence of remote code execution against an Apache mod_php installation running PHP 8.4.26. A CISA spokesperson couldn't immediately share more information about threat actors potentially chaining Fragnesia and PHP2Shell in attacks when BleepingComputer reached out earlier today. d71449.text: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) on Wednesday ordered nine food delivery, airline, ride-sharing and retail companies to turn over detailed information on how they harness personal data to set individual consumer prices and employee compensation. Orders were sent to JetBlue, Delta, United, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Walmart and Target, the agency said. If the companies don’t respond, the agency can force them to comply in federal court. The information will allow the agency to “assess whether the pricing for a ticket, ride share, food delivery or other product or service varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data by superintelligence algorithms,” the FTC said. The companies employing gig workers also must give the agency the “inputs, tools and procedures” they deploy to tweak individual workers’ compensation and customer pricing based on personal data and unique characteristics, the agency said. FTC officials plan to scrutinize the “opaque methodology” firms could be using to decide what to charge customers or pay individual gig workers, agency chair Andrew Ferguson said in a press release. Consumers deserve to know if firms exploit their online browsing or other personal data to determine the highest price they think a given customer is willing to pay and the lowest price they think an individual worker will accept, he said. Ride-share and food-delivery companies may compensate workers on a shifting basis using murky formulas that exploit drivers’ personal data, including phone usage and payments they have historically agreed to, the press release said. The nine firms have 45 days to respond to the orders. The FTC Act allows the agency to compel industry to turn over information for studies that do not have a specific law enforcement purpose. The FTC probe follows an order in July 2024 to eight companies seeking information about how they facilitated the alleged surveillance of consumers by third-party companies to create different pricing for the same products or services based on personal data. Days before leaving her position in January 2025, outgoing chair Lina Khan released preliminary findings, which were drawn from information provided by McKinsey & Co., Accenture, Revionics and five other firms. Ferguson subsequently objected to the Khan release, announced he was closing the probe and said he would not divulge the full findings. The prior study was shut down because it was based on information from “middlemen consultancies,” according to Wednesday’s press release. “The agency learned nothing about actual pricing decisions from the 2024 study,” it said. “This study corrects the commission’s mistaken 2024 approach and demands information directly from companies who may be engaging in personalized pricing, rather than middlemen.” The eight previously queried “middleman consultancies” allegedly sold surveillance pricing tools to businesses as opposed to setting algorithm-driven pricing themselves. In August, the FTC asked the public to comment on a proposed enforcement policy statement describing how the setting of prices based on the undisclosed use of consumers’ singular personal data may be unlawful under the FTC Act. No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

b2sg4z.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybersecurity Google on Wednesday took the wraps off Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. "It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching," Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, said. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index benchmark, Carbon leads with a score of 59, surpassing Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (58), OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55). One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also twice as likely to generate secure code versus Argon. Google also emphasized that Carbon attempts to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks by seeking human input in the face of ambiguity rather than "guessing or forcing a path forward," as well as resisting every evaluated attack attempt at indirect prompt injection. The debut of Gemini 4 Carbon comes less than a week after the tech giant unveiled Gemini 4 Argon. The release plan is similar to that of its predecessor, with the rollout currently limited to a subset of cyber defenders before expanding access to other trusted partners as part of its Fairwind Program. Google also said it's actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing. The development comes as OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, which it described as a fast, efficient model that "excels at communication and computer-based tasks." "GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra," OpenAI said. "GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user's task." Earlier this week, rival Anthropic also disclosed that an unreleased, internal research model uncovered critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used software. This included a one-click remote code execution in Google Chrome, a one-click exploit chain in Apple Safari that could be used to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and other sensitive data, an Android lock screen bypass, and a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw in the Windows HTTP.sys driver (CVE-2026-33096, CVSS score: 7.5). All the identified issues have been fixed by Google, Apple, and Microsoft. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic said. "These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

opdkc2.text: Belgium's finance ministry has taken its main online tax portal offline following a cyberattack, just days before a filing deadline for some taxpayers. The Federal Public Service Finance (FPS Finance), which oversees taxation and other financial administration, said Wednesday that it was investigating the extent of the attack and had temporarily suspended access to MyMinfin, the country's main online platform for managing tax and financial affairs. The shutdown comes ahead of an October 31 deadline for taxpayers reporting certain types of income. The agency said affected taxpayers would be given additional time to file their returns, with a revised deadline to be announced later. Belgian authorities have not identified who was behind the attack or disclosed how the hackers may have gained access to government systems. "Currently, there is no indication that a data breach has occurred or that any data has been stolen," FPS Finance said, adding that investigators were continuing to examine the possibility of data exposure. The agency said it had taken the affected services offline as a precaution while specialists assessed the impact of the attack and carried out technical work to secure its systems. Several other government applications remained fully or partially operational. The incident follows an earlier security alert this month that prompted Belgian authorities to temporarily shut down several government websites over concerns about a software vulnerability. At the time, FPS Finance said it had taken many of its websites offline as a precaution because of an "international security issue," without providing further details. The disruption coincided with a broader cybersecurity alert over two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used programming language, that could allow attackers to remotely execute malicious code on vulnerable servers. Several government websites across Europe were temporarily shut down while administrators worked to address the vulnerabilities. Belgian news outlet The Brussels Times reported that FPS Finance websites were among those affected. Belgium's national cybersecurity center said at the time that it had received no reports of successful attacks exploiting the flaws against Belgian websites. It remains unclear whether Wednesday's cyberattack was connected to the earlier security alert. Belgian authorities have not publicly established any link between the incidents. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

1xnlxu0.text: Microsoft released the KB5127936 preview cumulative update for Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 26H2, with 41 changes, including File Explorer and Cloud rebuild improvements. KB5127936 is a preview update that adds new features and fixes at the end of each month, letting IT admins and users test them before they roll out to the entire user base during next month's Patch Tuesday. However, unlike regular Patch Tuesday cumulative updates, monthly preview updates are optional and don't include security patches. The October 2026 preview update makes the File Explorer context menu faster and easier to customize, letting users choose which app extensions and commands appear and how they're organized. After you install KB5127936, Cloud rebuild can also reinstall Windows without USB media or a custom image, using an image and drivers downloaded directly from Windows Update, even when Windows won't start. Microsoft also updated XBOX mode to include a refreshed Gaming Task View with quick access to key system actions like Power Options and Exit to Desktop while gaming via a new navigation bar. Windows 11 KB5127936 preview update (BleepingComputer) ​You can install the KB5127936 preview update by downloading it from the Microsoft Update Catalog or by opening Settings, going to Windows Update, and selecting "Check for Updates." Because this is an optional update, you will need to click the "Download and install" link unless you have "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" enabled (which prompts the OS to install it automatically). Windows 11 KB5127936 highlights Once installed, this optional non-security update will upgrade Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2 devices to builds 26200.9818 and 26300.9818, respectively. The October 2026 preview update adds further changes and improvements, some of the more important ones highlighted below: New! This update improves the Privacy & security page in Windows Settings by grouping related Camera, Microphone, and Location privacy controls and elevating usage information from linked pages onto the main page. New! This update enables Windows recovery (WinRE) to automatically reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles already saved in Windows, including supported certificate-based networks. Devices can now get online automatically during recovery scenarios such as quick machine recovery or cloud rebuild, without preconfiguring Wi-Fi credentials in WinRE. This capability is on by default, and IT admins can disable it. Microsoft disclosed this feature last month, and it is now beginning to roll out. New! This update introduces a Restore Summary that appears after you restore a backup profile to a new device. The summary clearly shows what was restored, including Windows settings and the list of Microsoft Store apps. This improves transparency during device transitions, helps you validate your restore results, and lets you continue setup on your new device with confidence. New! This update improves the adaptive hibernate policy to provide faster Modern Standby instant-on resumes while helping preserve battery life when the charge is low. Noticeable changes include less hibernation when the battery is above 80% and earlier hibernation below 10%. This month, Microsoft also reminded users that updated Secure Boot certificates are rolling out to replace the original 2011 certificates, which will expire in late June 2027. Microsoft first announced plans to refresh expiring Secure Boot certificates on eligible Windows 11 systems in January, after warning users and IT admins in November 2025 to update them before they expire. The company also warned customers they may need to reboot one more time after installing the October 2026 optional update and updates rolling out over the next several months. "With recent and upcoming Windows updates over the next few months, a limited number of consumer and business devices might experience one additional restart during installation," Microsoft noted in a message center update. "This one‑time restart occurs after a Secure Boot certificate update is applied as part of the Secure Boot update process." 1kwmvaz.text: The Hacker NewsOct 29, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Webinar Security teams have spent years trying to detect threats faster. AI is changing the harder part: how much time defenders have left to act. Advanced AI models can now help attackers discover vulnerabilities, generate exploit code, and move through weaknesses faster than traditional security processes were built to handle. The challenge is no longer just finding another vulnerability or generating another alert. It is knowing which exposures matter, what an attacker can reach, and which issues need to be fixed first. That is the focus of next week's webinar, How to Build AI Threat Readiness Across Your Security Operations, featuring an expert from Wiz. The session will show how security teams can improve visibility, prioritize real risk, and shorten the path from detection to remediation. Most security teams already have plenty of data. They have vulnerability findings, cloud alerts, identity signals, application telemetry, and threat detections. The harder problem is connecting those signals quickly enough to answer the questions that drive action. Is this vulnerability reachable? Does the exposed asset contain sensitive data? Can an attacker move from it to something more important? Who owns the affected system? What should be fixed first? When those answers live across different tools and teams, investigations slow down. That delay matters more when attackers can automate parts of the discovery and exploitation process. The webinar focuses on two practical needs: broad visibility and faster action. Security teams need enough context to understand risk across cloud infrastructure, code, identities, SaaS, AI services, and the software supply chain. They also need a way to identify exploitable paths, investigate suspicious activity, and deliver remediation to the right owner without having to rebuild the same context every time. A Wiz expert will explain how organizations can use unified security context to separate urgent exposure from background noise, understand attack paths, and bring security agents into investigation and remediation workflows. For SOC teams, that can mean less time spent manually assembling context. For vulnerability management, it means knowing which findings deserve immediate attention. For cloud and security engineering teams, it means connecting risk to the people and systems that can actually fix it. The goal is not to automate every security decision. It is to remove delays caused by fragmented tools, repetitive investigation, and unclear ownership. Attendees will leave with a framework for assessing whether their current security operations are ready for faster, AI-assisted attacks. The key questions are practical: Can you see enough of the environment to understand an attack path? Can you quickly determine whether a new issue affects something attackers can reach? Can you move a validated risk from detection to remediation fast enough? AI is increasing the speed at which weaknesses can be found and used. Security teams need to respond with better context and less delay.

14ic6cu.text: A flaw in Telegram for Android allowed an attacker to run code on a victim's phone via a voice call once the victim answered, according to security startup NebuSec. The attacker needed only an ordinary Telegram account. Telegram fixed the flaw in version 12.10.4 of the app, released in late September, and NebuSec disclosed it on October 29. The flaw can be triggered in every version from 8.6.2 through 12.10.3, NebuSec's co-founder and chief executive said in an email to The Hacker News. Those versions came out between March 2022 and September 2026. The company confirmed it in private phone calls on ARM64-based phones and has no evidence so far that it directly affects Telegram's iOS and desktop apps or group calls. Anyone using Telegram for Android should make sure the app is on version 12.10.4 or later. The version number appears at the bottom of the app's Settings page. The flaw had no CVE identifier as of October 29. The Hacker News has asked NebuSec and Telegram whether the flaw was used in real attacks, and asked NebuSec what an attacker's code could reach on a phone. During a Telegram call, the two apps send each other short messages to set up the call and report its state. One type, called MediaState, reports whether the microphone is muted, whether the camera is on, and how the video is rotated. The flaw was in the code that reads MediaState messages. That code did not handle missing fields correctly and accessed memory it should not, according to NebuSec. Telegram's published source code for version 12.10.3 contains a flaw that matches that description, a review by The Hacker News found. When a MediaState message included a rotation value, the code checked that value. It then read a different field, the video state, even if the message had no such field. Version 12.10.4 reads the rotation value from the right field. The calling code that uses this message was switched on in version 8.6.2, the first version NebuSec names. Telegram's Android, iOS, and desktop apps use one shared library, called tgcalls, for calls. A change labeled "Fix camera rotation" made the same correction in tgcalls on April 21, 2026. Telegram's iOS source code included that change from version 12.7, released in May, and the desktop app's code from version 7.0.1, released in July. Telegram for Android received it in version 12.10.4 in September. Whether the earlier code could be exploited in those apps has not been shown. NebuSec's video shows two phones, one marked as the attacker and one as the victim. The victim accepts a Telegram call. About half a minute into the call, the victim's phone switches to its home screen, the app icons fall down the screen, and a "HACKED BY NEBUSEC" logo appears. The video does not show which Telegram or Android version the victim's phone was running. No technical write-up of the flaw was on NebuSec's website as of October 29, so the step from the flaw to running code depends on the video and on what the company says. NebuSec, a startup backed by Y Combinator, says its Code Security product, which runs on OpenAI's GPT-5.4 model, found the flaw. In July, the company described an Android exploit chain that started with a Firefox flaw and reached the kernel of an ARM64 device running Android 17. Separately, the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) published an advisory on October 15 about an unpatched flaw in rlottie, the library Telegram apps have used to draw animated stickers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111105 (CVSS score: 7.0), can let an attacker run code if a user opens a malicious file or page, ZDI said. Telegram had told ZDI in March that checks on its servers mitigated the flaw, and in April asked ZDI for a full remote code execution chain. Those checks could be bypassed, researcher Saifeldeen Aziz says in the abstract for his OffensiveCon talk in Tokyo. The research used AI-guided fuzzing, which feeds code with large amounts of broken or unexpected input, to find memory-corruption bugs in rlottie across Telegram's iOS, Android, and desktop apps. It then chained those bugs, which stem from flaws in how stickers are delivered and checked, to run code on Telegram for iOS. The Android app replaced rlottie with tlottie, a library written in Rust, between versions 12.8.1 in June and 12.10.0 in August, according to Telegram's published source code. The desktop app's code made the same switch in September, and the iOS code added tlottie in version 13.0 in October while still including rlottie.

1oodlak.text: AI is beginning to take over much of the work that has traditionally defined the security analyst's job. Investigating alerts, collecting evidence, correlating activity across tools, and executing response actions are becoming tasks that AI systems can perform on their own. As these capabilities mature, security operations centers (SOCs) will see major changes in how work is organized, how decisions are made, and what is expected of the people responsible for defending organizations. For security professionals, this is a chance to take on a much broader role. As AI assumes more of the operational workload, analysts can move beyond individual alerts and investigations to direct the defense across the entire security lifecycle. We call this emerging role the Threat Operator: an AI-native security professional who translates business risk into defensive priorities, directs AI-driven operations, and exercises judgment over the decisions and actions taken by those systems. The impact reaches beyond day-to-day SOC work. It will change the skills organizations need, how security professionals develop expertise, and the career paths open to people entering the field. From Individual Tasks to Overall Defense The traditional SOC developed around specialized functions, each supported by its own tools and workflows. Threat intelligence teams study adversaries, detection engineers create rules, threat hunters search for activity that existing controls may have missed, analysts investigate alerts, and incident responders contain confirmed threats. These functions are closely related, yet the work often moves between teams through separate systems, tickets, and manual handoffs. AI is starting to tie these activities together. For example, intelligence about a new threat can lead to a hunting hypothesis, which can reveal a detection gap and produce a new detection. That detection may identify suspicious activity requiring investigation, followed by containment and further improvements to the organization's defenses. AI agents can coordinate and execute these workflows, carrying context and findings from one stage to the next. That changes where security professionals add the most value. A Threat Operator works across the defensive lifecycle, setting priorities based on the organization's exposure, business operations, and threat landscape. They determine which risks deserve attention, what the defense should accomplish, how much autonomy AI should have, and when a decision requires human intervention. They are also responsible for judging whether the operation is actually improving security. Consider a financial institution facing a newly identified threat targeting identity infrastructure. AI agents could assess the institution's exposure, hunt for relevant activity, identify gaps in existing detections, and recommend defensive actions. The Threat Operator would provide the institutional context needed to guide that work, including which systems support critical business processes, what constitutes unacceptable risk, and which actions require authorization. The result is a gradual shift from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop, with security professionals supervising and governing AI-driven operations. The level of autonomy will depend on the maturity of the technology, the consequences of particular actions, and the organization's tolerance for risk, but a human remains accountable throughout. Rethinking How Security Professionals Gain Experience Junior security analysts will feel some of the biggest effects. For decades, the SOC has provided an entry point into cybersecurity, with analysts developing their skills through alert triage, evidence collection, investigations, documentation, and escalation. Although much of this work is repetitive, it has also served as an apprenticeship. Over time, analysts learn how systems behave, how attackers operate, and how experienced practitioners distinguish genuine threats from benign activity. As AI absorbs more of these responsibilities, organizations will need to rethink how that experience is acquired. The traditional progression from handling simple alerts to managing complex investigations may become less relevant as AI takes on more sophisticated work. Without a deliberate approach to training, security teams may struggle to develop the experienced professionals they will need in the future. AI can also open up a different path for professional development. Junior Threat Operators can gain supervised exposure to a much wider range of security activities, examining how intelligence informs hunting, how detections are developed, how investigations reach conclusions, and how response decisions affect the business. They can review the evidence behind AI-generated findings, challenge assumptions, identify missing context, and learn from the decisions made by more experienced colleagues. This only works if organizations invest in technical fundamentals and structured mentorship. Analysts still need to understand networks, operating systems, attacker techniques, and the security technologies underlying AI-driven workflows. Experienced practitioners will need to teach younger colleagues how to evaluate conclusions, recognize uncertainty, and exercise judgment when the available evidence is incomplete. The Skills Needed For the current generation of security analysts, technical proficiency has often been measured through familiarity with security tools and the ability to extract useful information from them. Query languages, detection logic, endpoint telemetry, and investigation techniques have been central to the profession. Those skills still matter. AI adds new demands on top of them: orchestration, governance, and interpreting automated decisions. Threat Operators will need to translate business security risks into clear defensive objectives that AI systems can execute. They must understand the organization's architecture, critical assets, operational dependencies, and relevant adversaries, and know how to communicate that context to AI agents. Their work will involve evaluating hypotheses, validating evidence, setting escalation criteria, and determining whether an automated action has achieved its intended outcome. For example, an AI system investigating a compromised server may recommend immediate isolation. That call could be technically sound. But the server may support a critical business process where disruption carries significant consequences. A Threat Operator must understand those dependencies and determine how the response should proceed, balancing containment requirements with operational risk. This need for defined oversight and accountability is also reflected in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The role will combine four areas of expertise: Business security risk: Understanding organizational priorities, critical assets, and the consequences of security decisions. Threat and adversary understanding: Interpreting intelligence and anticipating how attackers may target the environment. Defensive operations: Understanding detection, hunting, investigation, and response across the security lifecycle. AI orchestration and judgment: Directing AI workflows, evaluating their conclusions, and governing automated actions. Building a Career Path Around Defensive Outcomes The Threat Operator role should become a career path with increasing levels of responsibility. Early-career operators can focus on validating evidence, reviewing AI conclusions, adding environmental context, and understanding how decisions connect across the defensive lifecycle. As they gain experience, they can begin translating business risks into defensive objectives, directing agent workflows, identifying coverage gaps, and determining when operations should escalate or act. Senior Threat Operators will take responsibility for defining autonomy boundaries, governing consequential actions, evaluating the reliability of AI-driven decisions, and measuring whether security operations are reducing organizational risk. Professionals may enter this career path from investigations, threat intelligence, detection engineering, incident response, security architecture, or risk management, bringing different areas of expertise to a role that spans the entire defensive operation. Security leaders should start building the training, governance, and progression frameworks needed to support these responsibilities. That includes establishing which decisions require human approval, how operators validate AI-generated evidence, how autonomy expands as systems demonstrate reliability, and how individual performance is evaluated. Measures such as the quality of defensive decisions, the closure of detection gaps, and improvements in threat coverage will matter more alongside traditional operational metrics. This will happen at different speeds in different organizations. Security professionals will have more say in how their organizations defend themselves. The old SOC trained people to operate tools. The AI-native SOC has to train them to operate the defense. Conifers.ai’s CognitiveSOC platform uses agentic AI to connect threat intelligence, hunting, detection engineering, investigation, and response, and every agent action comes with a reasoning chain and evidence trail that analysts can review. Learn more about how Conifers helps security teams direct and govern AI-driven defense across the full SOC lifecycle.

wmb22b.text: 26,400 credentials that developers left in public code on Gitee, a Chinese code-hosting service, still worked when a researcher tested them. Anyone who copied one from that code could have used it. Independent researcher Ben Zimmermann found them by scanning 7.25 million public Gitee repositories and reported the results on October 28. Most were keys for cloud and AI services, led by 9,473 Alibaba Cloud AccessKey pairs. Zimmermann sent the vendors with the most exposed keys a list of their credentials, but he did not contact the developers who leaked them. When he published, he had not confirmed that any of the reported credentials had been revoked. So anyone who has pushed a key to a public Gitee repository cannot assume it has been revoked. The scan ran for about a month, but Zimmermann did not provide the dates, so it is unclear how long ago the credentials were tested. He also did not say whether anyone else had used them. He ran two secret scanners, TruffleHog and Kingfisher, over every repository. Both tried each credential against the service that issued it and kept only those that worked, he wrote. The scanners read each repository's full commit history. A key that a developer later removed from the code could still be found and counted there. The 26,400 figure counts each credential once, regardless of how many repositories it appeared in. By commit date, 12,242 of the credentials came from 2025, nearly half the total. Some dated to the late 2000s. What Was Exposed After the Alibaba Cloud keys, the largest groups were 3,805 YouTube API keys, 3,170 DeepSeek keys, 1,489 keys for Zhipu's BigModel AI platform, and 1,348 OpenAI keys. Smaller numbers were found for GitHub, AWS, Google Cloud and Google's Gemini. One of the credentials was "an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform," Zimmermann wrote. He did not name the platform or say what the credential could reach. What a working key lets someone do depends on the service. OpenAI says that a compromised key allows another person to use the account's quota without the owner's consent. That can cause "data loss, unexpected charges," a used-up monthly quota, and interrupted API access. A YouTube API key is a Google Cloud API key that identifies a project, Google says. Without API restrictions, such a key can be used with every API that accepts Google Cloud keys. What to Do If You Committed Keys Treat any key that has ever been in a public Gitee repository as exposed, and revoke it at the provider. Deleting a key from the code or rewriting the repository's history does not revoke it, as noted by TruffleHog's maker, Truffle Security. Alibaba Cloud: create a new AccessKey pair, switch your apps to it, then disable and delete the old pair. Check for unexpected charges and for resources created or deleted that you did not need, Alibaba Cloud's leak response plan says. ActionTrail shows the key's API calls for the last 90 days, but data operations in services such as OSS and SLS have to be checked in each service's own logs. Google and YouTube API keys: rotate the key, which creates a new key with the same restrictions, update your apps to use it, then delete the old key. Add API restrictions so the key works only with the APIs you need. OpenAI: rotate the key immediately from the API Keys page, as OpenAI advises, and set spend limits to help limit charges from a leaked key. Two Scanners, Different Results MongoDB makes Kingfisher, and Zimmermann's post was developed with its Kingfisher team. In this scan, TruffleHog found 12,737 credentials that worked, and Kingfisher found 14,664, but only 1,001 were found by both. Each tool alone found about half of the total. TruffleHog found almost all of the Alibaba Cloud keys. Kingfisher found all 1,489 BigModel keys, because TruffleHog has no detector for Zhipu's keys, Zimmermann wrote. Teams that rely on a single scanner should verify its detectors against the services they use. Gitee and Other Code Hosts China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology chose Gitee in 2020 as the base for a national open-source code-hosting platform. Gitee's public API is limited, and a 2021 attempt to study leaked credentials on the site gave up because of it. Gitee's rate, 3.64 working credentials per 1,000 repositories scanned, is higher than the rates from earlier scans of GitLab (3.11) and Bitbucket (2.39). Those scans used only TruffleHog, Zimmermann wrote. Based on TruffleHog's results alone, Gitee's rate is 1.76, but that count excludes services TruffleHog does not cover, such as Zhipu. So neither figure shows which platform leaks more.

1kovp.text: Cisco released security updates to patch a denial-of-service zero-day in Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Threat Defense (FTD) software that attackers are exploiting to remotely crash vulnerable firewall devices. Tracked as CVE-2026-76418, this high-severity vulnerability affects devices running ASA and FTD software with configurations containing the 'webvpn' keyword and SSL VPN enabled on at least one interface. Successful exploitation allows unauthenticated, remote attackers to trigger a denial-of-service (DoS) condition, causing the device to reload unexpectedly. Cisco advised customers to patch vulnerable firewalls after its Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) discovered evidence that the flaw was being exploited in the wild earlier this month. However, the company didn't provide indicators of compromise and hasn't shared additional information about the attacks, including which organizations are being targeted or who is exploiting the flaw. "This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition," Cisco said. "In October 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability. Cisco strongly recommends that customers upgrade to a fixed software release to remediate this vulnerability." While Cisco provided no workarounds that address this security issue, admins who can't immediately patch CVE-2026-76418 can mitigate it by disabling secondary authentication on the default DefaultWEBVPNGroup tunnel group or on any user-configured tunnel group list. Currently, Internet monitoring platform Shadowserver tracks more than 51,000 Cisco ASA SSL VPN devices exposed online, but doesn't provide information on how many have already been secured or are honeypots. Internet-exposed Cisco ASA SSL VPN devices (Shadowserver) ​Last year, Cisco patched two other flaws (CVE-2025-20362 and CVE-2025-20333) affecting ASA and FTD firewall devices in September and cautioned customers that attackers had exploited them in zero-day attacks targeting 5500-X Series devices with VPN web services enabled. The same day, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued Emergency Directive 25-03, ordering federal agencies to secure their Cisco firewall devices within 24 hours. Cisco linked the attacks to the ArcaneDoor campaign, which had also been exploiting two other zero-days (CVE-2024-20353 and CVE-2024-20359) to breach government networks since November 2023. More recently, in August, Cisco addressed another denial-of-service zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2026-20349) that attackers were actively exploiting in the wild to crash affected ASA and FTD firewall devices with SSL listen sockets enabled. Earlier this month, it also warned customers to patch an actively exploited zero-day (CVE-2026-76519) in its Secure Email Gateway (SEG) security solution that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands remotely with root privileges. Since November 2021, CISA has flagged 101 Cisco security flaws as exploited in the wild, seven of which were also abused by ransomware gangs.
