18rwc5.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Cisco has released patches to address a high-severity security flaw in Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software that it said has been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76418, is rated 8.6 on the CVSS scoring system. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. According to Cisco, the issue is rooted in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of ASA and FTD software. "This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group," it said in a Wednesday advisory. "An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition." The network equipment major said it became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability in October 2026, but did not share any specifics as to when the attacks began, who is behind them, and the scale of the efforts. Fixes for the flaw are available in the following versions - Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software Release 9.16 and earlier - Fixed in 9.16.4.104 9.18 - Fixed in 9.18.4.96 9.20 - Fixed in 9.20.4.50 9.22 - Fixed in 9.22.3.200 9.23 - Fixed in 9.23.1.48 9.24 - Fixed in 9.24.1.27 and 9.24.10.1 Cisco Secure FTD Software Release 7.0 and earlier - Fixed in 7.0.11 7.2 - Fixed in 7.2.13 7.4 - Fixed in 7.4.9 7.6 - Fixed in 7.6.7 7.7 - Fixed in 7.7.14 10.0 - Fixed in 10.0.3 10.1 - Fixed in 10.1.1 Cisco also noted that the vulnerability affects Cisco devices if the following conditions are met - They are running a vulnerable release of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software or Cisco Secure FTD Software. The SSL remote access VPN login service is reachable. Secondary authentication is configured in the tunnel group scope. "If tunnel-group-list enable is configured, check all tunnel groups, including the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup, for secondary-authentication-server-group," Cisco said. "If tunnel-group-list enable is absent or has been removed using the no tunnel-group-list enable command, check the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup, for secondary-authentication-server-group because disabling the group list does not remove exposure when that default group uses secondary authentication." As a temporary mitigation, the company is recommending that customers turn off the tunnel group list if DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication, or disable secondary authentication on any user-configured tunnel group list or on the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup. "On Cisco Secure FTD Software, review the deployed remote access VPN policy and the resulting device running configuration in Cisco Secure FMC Software or Cisco Secure FDM," Cisco said. "A successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path." The disclosure comes as Cisco revealed that a sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor tracked as UAT-11473 weaponized CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances, to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems. The activity, which has targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research sectors, is assessed to share infrastructure overlaps with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train covert network. "UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as 'KeyDrift' consisting of multiple components [like PolyFlame and LittleFilch] geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts," Cisco Talos said. "The framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records."

1mol1hm.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026DevSecOps / Vulnerability GitHub has announced that it's introducing a new package firewall as a preview to block installation of suspicious npm packages during installation time. "The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate," GitHub said. The feature, which currently supports only npm packages, is available in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud. According to the Microsoft subsidiary, the firewall is placed between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories so as to deter malware attacks that compromise systems when packages are installed. This behavior can expose users to severe security risks, especially when artificial intelligence (AI) agents and CI runners automatically install dependencies to complete a task or build without their explicit permission. The idea is that endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of directly pointing to the public package registries. The firewall then checks package downloads against policy controls such as minimum package age and malware advisories, and blocks downloads that do not meet those policies. To use the firewall, administrators are required to configure policy controls, such as the ones listed below - Block known malware by checking against the GitHub Advisory Database for active malware advisories Block packages based on the severity of vulnerabilities by checking the GitHub Advisory Database for flaws that affect the requested package version. The control defaults to "Critical only" as the severity level that blocks an installation, although users can choose "High or higher," "Medium or higher," or "Any severity." Block attestation downgrades by comparing attestations for the requested package version with those of earlier versions and stop the download if the requested version does not have an SLSA attestation. Block newly-introduced install scripts by checking whether the package recently added scripts that run using preinstall or postinstall hooks, which can be abused to steal sensitive data. Block packages based on a cooldown period that prevents versions that are newer than the configured minimum age from being installed. The value can range from 1 to 365 days. The default value is 1 day. Users can disable it by setting it to 0. Users who need access to a package that gets blocked erroneously by the firewall can submit an exception request, which can then be approved by enterprise administrators and security managers. The development comes as Rust 1.100, which is scheduled for release on November 12, 2026, readies to add support for a configurable minimum publish age, allowing security scanners and maintainers time to flag and block malicious crate releases before they can be installed or used by users. The value, defined via the "global-min-publish-age" option in "cargo/config.toml," allows users to specify a minimum publication age in days or weeks. If left unspecified, a seven-day waiting period is applied by default to skip releases published within that window. Over the past year, similar waiting periods have been implemented across open-source ecosystems, including npm, Python, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Ruby, Bun, pnpm, and Yarn, as a way to bolster software supply chain security by reducing the chance that a newly published, unreviewed version is immediately pulled into a build. Cooldown periods help add friction and slow down attacks in which a bad actor publishes a poisoned version of a popular package after seizing control of a maintainer account, thereby preventing rapid spread through manual or automated installations. "The tradeoff is that legitimate fixes have to wait, too, unless developers make an exception," Socket said. "Malicious code also doesn't magically become harmless with age. A release that escapes detection can simply outlast the cooldown. The value is in buying researchers, maintainers, and registries time to act before the next dependency update carries an attack further."

1awwoq8.text: An attacker tried to exploit a critical GitLab vulnerability on the Alpine Linux project's own GitLab server a week after GitLab released a fix, Alpine Linux said on 28 October. The flaw, CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score: 10.0), can let an attacker run code on a GitLab server through a crafted regular expression in a CI configuration. Alpine found no evidence that the attack worked but cannot rule it out, so it rebuilt the server from scratch and reset every account's password. GitLab's fix is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab ships in its own packages and container images. Alpine's GitLab image used standard Ruby, so upgrading the server to GitLab 19.3.6 on 22 October did not fix the flaw. For anyone running GitLab on their own Ruby, built from source or in their own container image, "upgrading GitLab is not enough," Alpine said. Those servers also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later, and users of Alpine's alpinelinux/gitlab image need to pull 19.3.6 again. The server gitlab.alpinelinux.org hosts aports, the repository from which Alpine's packages are built. Packages built from 20 to 24 October, and the 21 October releases, came from aports changes verified against records outside GitLab, according to Alpine. Those releases include the minirootfs files that the official Alpine Docker images are built from. Alpine is extending the checks to 27 October, when it closed the server. The keys that sign its packages and releases have never been on the GitLab server. How the Attack Unfolded On 13 October, Alpine upgraded the server to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of 19.3.5, which it calls a mistake. The server was still on that version, without the 12 October fix, when a newly registered account began probing it on 20 October. The account sent crafted CI configurations to the server on 20 and 21 October. They crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times, and the main attack on 21 October also caused 502 errors and caused CI jobs to fail. In 4 of those crashes, the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step, according to Alpine. The attacker also downloaded Alpine's GitLab container image, which Alpine said: "suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build." Alpine blocked the account on 23 October. The attacker came back on 25 and 26 October and tried to get back in, but those attempts failed, Alpine said. On 26 October, Alpine found that the server was still vulnerable after its 22 October upgrade to 19.3.6. The next day, it closed GitLab to everyone except its developers and build servers and started rebuilding it. The rebuild finished on 28 October. Alpine also replaced GitLab's secret keys, and the rebuilt server runs Ruby 3.3.13 or later, which has the fix. Alpine is testing it before reopening it to the public. What Alpine Can and Cannot Rule Out Alpine found no sign that the attacker's code ran on the server. Timing probes showed no delays;; there were no unexpected files, keys, hooks, or processes; and no private data was sent back to the attacker via any web or API request that Alpine can see. It cannot be sure, though. "A successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs," Alpine said. Some logs from the attack day are gone, including background job logs and the old container's filesystem, and neither Alpine nor its hosting provider logged outbound network connections. Because the evidence needed to confirm code execution no longer exists, Alpine treated the server as compromised and rebuilt it to remove any foothold a successful exploit could have left. If the attack succeeded, these could have been exposed: Email addresses, names, and IP addresses of all users Password hashes 2FA secrets, CI/CD variables and runner tokens Webhook, integration and push mirror credentials Personal access tokens, which are stored as hashes Private repositories, and confidential issues and merge requests Beyond the password reset and the new secret keys, Alpine has not said whether runner tokens, CI/CD variables, access tokens or integration credentials stored on the server have been replaced. To check its packages, Alpine confirmed that every aports change added from 20 to 22 October arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. It checked this against records it says the attacker could not reach: a developer's copy of the repository and all 45 build servers. Every package built from 20 to 24 October came from aports changes as published on git.alpinelinux.org. Why the GitLab Upgrade Did Not Fix It GitLab compiles the regular expressions in CI configurations with Ruby, and the bug behind CVE-2026-97229 is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab's 12 October release fixed it by patching the Ruby inside GitLab's Linux package and container images. Ruby's own fixed versions came out on 22 and 23 October. A GitLab upgrade does not change a server's own Ruby, so a GitLab install on standard Ruby keeps the flaw until Ruby itself is updated to a fixed version, as Alpine found. GitLab's fixed Linux packages and its official container images carry the patched Ruby. A self-compiled install, or a container image that installs Ruby separately as Alpine's did, does not get it. As of 29 October, neither of GitLab's patch release posts for 12 and 21 October tells administrators of self-compiled installs to update Ruby. GitLab's self-compiled installation guide still lists Ruby 3.2 as its minimum version, and Ruby 3.2 reached end of life in April and will get no fix. Which GitLab Servers Are Exposed GitLab's advisory says that, "under certain conditions," the flaw could have allowed an unauthenticated user to run code on the server. GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already patched. Rapid7 built a working exploit in a lab and published proof-of-concept code on 13 October. The exploit ran commands as GitLab's git user on an unpatched official GitLab 19.4.1 image, but the same input did not run on the patched 19.4.2 image. That exploit needs write access first: the attacker must commit a malicious .gitlab-ci.yml file and a file path with UTF-8 characters to a branch of a public project. That requirement does not apply on servers where new users can register themselves and create projects. In Rapid7's tested route, "only the final CI lint request is unauthenticated." GitLab's own detection notes also say the attacker must first create that file path through ordinary repository APIs. Rapid7 does not yet know how the attack in the original report to GitLab, which is still private, avoids the write step. Alpine has not said how its attacker's CI configurations reached GitLab, or whether new accounts could create public projects on its server. CVE-2026-97229 was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the catalog's 28 October update. What GitLab Administrators Should Do GitLab's 21 October releases are the newest on each branch listed below, and they also fix CVE-2026-110264, a separate regex flaw. Branch Fixes CVE-2026-97229, per GitLab's advisory Newest release (21 October) 19.5 Not listed as affected 19.5.1 19.4 19.4.2 19.4.3 19.3 19.3.5 19.3.6 19.2 19.2.8 19.2.9 19.1, 19.0 and 18.11 Not listed as affected 19.1.9, 19.0.10 and 18.11.13 Which release fixes a server depends on how GitLab is installed: GitLab's Linux package or official container images: upgrade to the newest release for your branch. Self-compiled installs, or images that install their own Ruby: upgrade GitLab and update Ruby to 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9, or later. Ruby 3.2 will not receive the fix, so servers running 3.2 need to upgrade to one of those versions. GitLab's advisory named 19.3.4 as the fixed version for the 19.3 branch when it was published on 12 October. It now names 19.3.5 and lists 19.3.4 as affected, so servers still on 19.3.4 should move to 19.3.6. If a server cannot be upgraded right away, Rapid7 suggests restricting anonymous access to public projects, stopping untrusted users from creating or writing to public projects, or blocking the CI lint route. Those steps cover only Rapid7's exploit route and do not fix the vulnerable regular expression compiler, the company said. GitLab has published six detection rules for exploitation attempts against self-managed servers, written in the Sigma format. Four of them, which GitLab marks as experimental, look for hostile patterns in CI regexp warnings and GraphQL ciLint requests, unusually long file paths with non-ASCII characters, and Ruby crash reports that point to Onigmo. The guidance with those rules warns that a successful exploit can leave no crash, and it gives these further steps: Look for files owned by the git user in /tmp, unexpected child processes of Puma or Sidekiq, outbound connections, and changed crontabs or SSH keys for the git user. If there are signs of code execution, treat the server as compromised and rotate the secrets in gitlab-secrets.json, all CI/CD variables, all runner tokens and all access tokens. Limit who can create accounts and personal access tokens on the server. What Alpine Users Should Do Account holders will need to set a new password with "Forgot your password?" on the sign-in page when gitlab.alpinelinux.org reopens, Alpine said. It has also seen automated login attempts against its GitLab using passwords leaked from other sites, and anyone who used their gitlab.alpinelinux.org password elsewhere should change it there. Users of the alpinelinux/gitlab image should pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on 27 October contains Ruby 3.3.13, while any 19.3.6 image pulled before then, and every older tag, is vulnerable. Alpine's own Ruby packages already have the fix: Ruby 3.4.12 on Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge, and Ruby 3.3.13 on Alpine 3.21. Running apk upgrade installs it. Ruby's maintainers say the bug matters only for programs that compile a regular expression from text an attacker controls, and that Ruby's Regexp.timeout setting does not protect against it.

16cjjoc.text: Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN flaw, fixed in February, to plant custom malware inside the systems that control an organization's SD-WAN network. The malware, called KeyDrift, is designed to copy the keys that encrypt traffic between sites and store them for later use, Cisco Talos said on October 28. Talos calls the attacks historical but does not specify when they occurred or whether any keys were sent. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-20127 and has a CVSS score of 10.0. It allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and gain administrative privileges on these control systems. On a Controller, the attacker can log in as a high-privileged internal account that is not root. When Cisco disclosed the flaw in February, Talos tracked its exploitation as UAT-8616, a cluster of activity it said went back to at least 2023. In Cisco's traditional key exchange, each SD-WAN router periodically generates an AES key for its traffic and sends it to the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart). The Controller passes the keys on to other routers. A process on the Controller called vdaemon runs the encrypted control connections that carry these keys. On a compromised Controller, a KeyDrift component called LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted. For a preset list of edge routers, it pulls out their IP addresses and a 32-byte field. Talos assesses that field as the AES-256 key material that the Controller passes between routers. LittleFilch encrypts what it collects with RSA and writes it to a file. It can then send that data over UDP to an address listed in a settings file, which it deletes after reading. Talos could not recover that settings file. The group behind KeyDrift, which Talos tracks as UAT-11473, has targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research. The group's infrastructure "overlaps considerably" with Silent Train, Talos assesses with high confidence. Silent Train is the name Lumen's Black Lotus Labs uses for a network of hacked small-office, home-office, IoT and business devices. Lumen says Volt Typhoon used the network to hide its activity. CISA, the NSA and the FBI said in 2024 that Volt Typhoon is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber group. Talos links UAT-11473 to Volt Typhoon only through the infrastructure overlap. It does not say the two are the same group, or how UAT-11473 relates to UAT-8616, the cluster it reported in February. Separately, Lumen said on October 28 that Volt Typhoon was exploiting CVE-2026-20127 by late 2025 and continued to exploit it after Cisco disclosed the flaw in February. Lumen does not tie that activity to KeyDrift. KeyDrift primarily starts via modified runit scripts that Cisco SD-WAN devices use to launch their services, according to Talos. In one version, the script for the SSH service starts a loader script, conf_sshd, before the real SSH server. The conf_sshd script writes vdaemon's process IDs to a file, and a tool called rsshd injects KeyDrift's main module, PolyFlame, into each of those processes. PolyFlame runs in memory inside vdaemon. It can act as a TinyShell-like backdoor that runs commands and reads and writes files, or as a relay that forwards commands between its command server and other machines. It is built to accept commands within SD-WAN control traffic, and the analyzed samples contained no hardcoded server address. On a compromised Validator, formerly vBond, a fake aaamgr service under /etc/sv/aaamgr/ runs a packed loader, aaamgrd, that decrypts and runs PolyFlame. Cisco's real aaamgr component is a Python package and does not normally run as a compiled service. There are also signs of timestomping: commands the group ran copied the timestamps and permissions of existing files onto its own files. Affected Releases and Fixes CVE-2026-20127 affects the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart), Manager (formerly vManage), and Validator (formerly vBond), regardless of their configuration. On-premises systems are affected, as are Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments, including the Cisco Managed and FedRAMP environments. Cisco added the Validator to its advisory on June 16. Cisco says it is aware of limited exploitation of the flaw. There is no workaround, and the first fixed releases are: Release train First fixed release Earlier than 20.9 Migrate to a fixed release 20.9 20.9.8.2 20.11 20.12.6.1 20.12 20.12.5.3 or 20.12.6.1 20.13 20.15.4.2 20.14 20.15.4.2 20.15 20.15.4.2 20.16 20.18.2.1 20.18 20.18.2.1 Releases earlier than 20.9 and the 20.11, 20.13, 20.14 and 20.16 trains have reached end of software maintenance. Until they can upgrade, on-premises customers can limit access to ports 22 and 830 to the IP addresses of known controllers and other known systems. Cisco says this step worked in a test environment, but that customers should check how well it works in their own networks. Such guardrails are already in place for Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments. Blocking the ports does not remove malware already on a device. Checking for KeyDrift Talos advises organizations to install Cisco's fixes, follow Cisco's Catalyst SD-WAN hardening guide and watch for signs of post-compromise activity. Anyone who finds such signs should start incident response and can ask Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC) for help. That advice does not say whether upgrading removes KeyDrift from a device that was already compromised, or whether any keys should be replaced. Cisco's February remediation guide for this flaw warns that there could be "existing exploits which are still in place" from before an upgrade. KeyDrift uses these files and locations, some given only by name: File: the run script under etc/sv/sshd/, modified to start conf_sshd Directory: /etc/sv/aaamgr/, a fake service on a compromised Validator File: aaamgrd, the packed loader File: conf_sshd, the loader script File: rsshd, the injector File: libdssl.so, PolyFlame File: libcommon.so, LittleFilch File: /tmp/system-vdaemon, the list of vdaemon process IDs File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, LittleFilch's encrypted records File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.conf, LittleFilch's send settings, deleted after reading Talos's report does not include a list of file hashes, IP addresses or domains for KeyDrift. Talos released Snort rules on October 28 that look for inbound KeyDrift command-and-control connections: 67387 through 67416 for Snort 2, and 7:44 through 7:73 for Snort 3. Rules 65938 and 65958, already available, cover CVE-2026-20127 itself. The October 28 rule update lists the Snort 2 rules as disabled by default, so users of the paid Snort Subscriber rule set must turn them on. The Snort 3 rules appear with no default state. To check for exploitation of the flaw itself, Cisco says to look in /var/log/auth.log for Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin entries from unknown IP addresses. Before opening a TAC case, customers should run request admin-tech on each control component. The remediation guide also recommends rescanning those admin-tech files with the Check Bug Applicability feature on the Bug Search Tool page for bug CSCws52722. For US federal civilian agencies, CISA's February 25 emergency directive sets out what to do if a root account compromise is found. They must report it to CISA, deploy fresh Manager, Controller and Validator instances from patched images, and move their edge routers to the new systems.

1j3l637.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Espionage The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a security flaw impacting Broadcom VMware ESX to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, after CrowdStrike revealed that it had been weaponized by a China-nexus threat actor known as Warp Panda in attacks targeting the U.S. legal sector. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an insufficient logging vulnerability that could permit a malicious actor with admin access to perform certain operations without being logged. In an advisory released in July 2026, Broadcom revealed that the issue was addressed in the following versions - VMware Cloud Foundation SXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 and ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025 VMware vSphere Foundation SXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 and ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025 VMware ESX ESXi80U3j-25429389 VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.4 VMware Telco Cloud Platform ESXi80U3j-25429389 The development comes in response to CrowdStrike's 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report, which revealed that Warp Panda had exploited CVE-2026-41709 as a zero-day in early 2026 with an aim to reduce audit trail visibility. Warp Panda "exploits internet-facing edge devices using zero-day vulnerabilities and custom malware to maintain covert, persistent access," it said in the report shared with The Hacker News, adding the adversary "actively circumvents detection by bypassing audit logging, harvesting cloud session tokens, and registering rogue multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices." The threat actor, also tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), Clay Typhoon, and VerdantBamboo, has a storied history of weaponizing zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure devices. Earlier this month, Google-owned Mandiant also attributed the hacking crew to the zero-day exploitation of a critical improper origin validation in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deliver malware families like SAWFLY and BARECLAW. Attacks mounted by Warp Panda involve the exploitation of internet-facing edge devices to obtain initial access, after which the threat actor pivots to VMware vCenter environments to deploy custom malware like BRICKSTORM and SharpStorm to maintain persistent access without attracting attention. Select intrusions have also involved the targeting of cloud services with an aim to extract user session tokens to access Microsoft 365 environments sans raising any credential-based alerts. In at least one case, Warp Panda is said to have registered a new MFA device on a compromised account as a way to set up persistent access even if the password is changed. "Warp Panda represents a sustained and strategically focused China-nexus cyber espionage threat to U.S. entities across multiple sectors, including the legal sector," CrowdStrike said. "The legal sector's concentration of client communications, merger and acquisition materials, active litigation strategy, and cross-client access makes it a high-value collection target for a state-directed adversary seeking intelligence with downstream operational utility." In light of active exploitation of CVE-2026-41709, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 11, 2026.

cl1q9x.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Palo Alto Networks on Wednesday warned that threat actors are exploiting the recently patched PHP2Shell vulnerabilities against publicly-accessible management interfaces. "Active exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet," the network security company said in an update to its advisory. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2), allow attackers to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on systems running affected versions of PHP. The issues were patched upstream by the PHP Foundation on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The development comes days after Israeli cybersecurity company Dream said it observed a suspected China-nexus threat actor weaponizing the flaws in conjunction with a local privilege escalation bug in the Linux kernel, tracked as Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300, CVSS score: 7.8), to root 25 servers across the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Among those were three systems belonging to a U.S. government-affiliated environment. "The affected devices run specific versions of a large vendor's firewall software," Dream noted. "The attacker then launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration." Although Dream did not disclose the name of the affected firewall vendor, the timing of the advisory, combined with the fact that other network security companies have not reported malicious exploitation against their products, suggests that these events may be related. The Hacker News has contacted both Dream and Palo Alto Networks for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back. The development has prompted the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add CVE-2026-46300 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 31, 2026. "This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP web shells and run commands as root," CISA said. Palo Alto Networks has also noted that no special configuration is required to be affected by this issue, adding the risk is highest on PAN-OS when access to the management interface is allowed from external IP addresses on the internet. "This issue strictly affects the management web interface, which includes the HTTPS web UI and XML API service," it said. "It affects the dataplane interface only if a management profile is attached to it." The following versions of PAN-OS are impacted by PHP2Shell - PAN-OS 12.2 < 12.2.4-h1 (Fixed in >= 12.2.4-h1) PAN-OS 12.1 < 12.1.4-h13 (Fixed in >= 12.1.4-h13) (ETA: 10/29) < 12.1.7-h11 (Fixed in >= 12.1.7-h11) < 12.1.10-h3 (Fixed in >= 12.1.10-h3) (ETA: 10/30) PAN-OS 11.2 < 11.2.4-h23 (Fixed in >= 11.2.4-h23) (ETA: 10/30) < 11.2.7-h23 (Fixed in >= 11.2.7-h23) < 11.2.10-h16 (Fixed in >= 11.2.10-h16) < 11.2.13-h4 (Fixed in >= 11.2.13-h4) < 11.2.16-h1 (Fixed in >= 11.2.16-h1) PAN-OS 11.1 < 11.1.4-h38 (Fixed in >= 11.1.4-h38) < 11.1.6-h40 (Fixed in >= 11.1.6-h40) < 11.1.7-h12 (Fixed in >= 11.1.7-h12) (ETA: 10/30) < 11.1.10-h36 (Fixed in >= 11.1.10-h36) < 11.1.13-h16 (Fixed in >= 11.1.13-h16) < 11.1.16-h4 (Fixed in >= 11.1.16-h4) PAN-OS 10.2 < 10.2.7-h39 (Fixed in >= 10.2.7-h39) (ETA: 10/30) < 10.2.10-h42 (Fixed in >= 10.2.10-h42) (ETA: 10/29) < 10.2.13-h27 (Fixed in >= 10.2.13-h27) < 10.2.16-h12 (Fixed in >= 10.2.16-h12) < 10.2.18-h13 (Fixed in >= 10.2.18-h13) For PAN-OS versions where fix versions are not yet available, Palo Alto Networks has recommended the following mitigations - Route incoming traffic for the MGT port through a DP port, e.g., enabling management profile on a DP interface for management access. Replace the Certificate for Inbound Traffic Management. Decrypt inbound traffic to the management interface so the firewall can inspect it. Enable threat prevention on the inbound traffic to management services. "Customers with Frontier Virtual Patching (ATP Plus) on PAN-OS 12.2.4 and later versions received advance coverage, released via Threat ID 543004, which was released at 10:21 PM PT on October 20," it said. "The security risk posed by this issue on PAN-OS and Panorama is minimized by restricting access to the management interface to only trusted internal IP addresses according to our recommended best practice deployment guidelines."

1m78iax.text: U.S. law enforcement has seized the primary domain of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service advertised on cybercrime forums for facilitating illegal activities. The service also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, and promised to shield customers from legal complaints and requests from law enforcement and other authorities. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) confirmed that Virtualine marketed services that permitted “illegal/black hat activities” ranging from phishing, spamming, and carding to port scanning. The FBI seized the primary domain of the service, virtualine[.net], following an investigation that involved Germany’s Polizei Hessen, the Netherlands’ Politie Midden-Nederland, the U.K.’s National Crime Agency, as well as private partners OverRIPE and Lumen. Seizure banner Source: BleepingComputer Although Virtualine drew an apparent line at child content, authorities say that the operator knowingly hosted an online forum promoting child abuse material and ignored repeated notices from law enforcement, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and a victim’s attorney. Authorities allege that after legal pressure against the forum increased, Virtualine worked with the administrators to set up a new site. "Virtualine hosts this new website to this day, and it has already received at least one abuse complaint about sexually explicit images of children found on that website," the DoJ said. The administrator of the Virtualine rejected the allegation in an open letter to authorities published on a new website, virtualine[.]org, captured by cybersecurity company Silent Push. The operator said that while claims about the service's illegal activities and customers "deserve a fair investigation," they regarded "sexual exploitation of children as a crime against humanity." Cybercrime ecosystem Virtualine also accepted direct Bitcoin payments from customers, helping cybercriminals launder proceeds stolen elsewhere. Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, which provided intelligence support to law enforcement, linked Virtualine’s payment addresses directly to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, scams, and phishing platforms. “Virtualine accepted direct bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without flagging their funds through hosted exchange compliance programs,” Chainalysis notes. “Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin,” the blockchain company added. In a report published today, blockchain intelligence firm TRM said ransomware groups were responsible for 5% of Virtualine’s financial flows, while a Russian drug marketplace made up approximately 44%. "A large sextortion scheme and a mixer were also major sources of funds," the company said. Virtualine customers source: TRM TRM says that Virtualine also received payments from the StealC infostealer this year, with transactions indicating a constant financial relationship. A press release from the Dutch police notes that dozens of physical servers were seized in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline. Politie also said its investigators recovered data from more than 3,000 Virtualine customers, and follow-up action against them is underway. According to the authorities in the Netherlands, the illegal platform was facilitating cybercrime operations since at least 2022, including ransomware, botnets, infostealers, phishing, and distribution of child abuse material. Although the bulletproof hosting provider remains partially online, researchers observed that its network prefixes currently have very low routing visibility, suggesting that much of its infrastructure may no longer be reachable. 1djndeb.text: Discord will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation. The goal is to surface useful information to the wider internet community instead of keeping it buried in Discord conversations. “Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you’re looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord,” the messaging platform explains. The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers, publicly listed communities with at least 1,000 members. The platform says it hosts approximately 63,000 such servers. This decision excludes private servers, direct messages between users, and group announcements on servers that don’t meet the requirements. According to the company's schedule, the rollout will happen in two stages: On November 16, every Discoverable Server will get a public Server Web Page which will display automatically generated summaries of active conversations from that date onward. Starting mid-December, every eligible message posted on Discoverable Servers will appear on the Server Web Page and may be indexed by web search engines. Server Web Pages will be automatically created on November 16 if admins haven’t created them by then, and the only way to avoid them is to change the server type to private before the cutoff date. Discord has been piloting Community Messages and Server Web Pages in the NBA 2K, Rust, and Dead by Daylight gaming groups. Dead by Daylight Server Web Page Source: Discord The December rollout will be gradual, and Discord says messages posted before the release date will be excluded. Channel administrators can choose to exclude individual channels or turn off all channel content sharing entirely using controls available under Server Settings > Web Presence. Administrator data exposure setting Source: Discord Community members can also control if their messages appear on the Server Web Page through User Settings > Data and Privacy. However, changing that setting only affects future messages, and past messages that became public cannot be retracted. User data privacy setting Source: Discord If admins and users leave the settings at their defaults, their content will automatically be included in the new sharing scheme. However, message sharing will stay off by default in all EU countries, the UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea. In those places, members must explicitly enable it in their privacy settings. Underage users are automatically excluded and cannot activate the feature until they turn 18. 1v6eiq4.text: The China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Volt Typhoon has been attributed to a now-disrupted covert access network dubbed Silent Train that has been put to use for zero-day exploitation and strategic access. "First identified in late 2023, Silent Train uses rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise infrastructure," Lumen Technologies Black Lotus Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It employs anti-forensic techniques, compartmentalized operations, and post-operation cleanup to minimize detection and attribution." Its main purpose is to facilitate critical attack phases like vulnerability exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration, and to maintain continued access to victim environments. The activity stands out for two main reasons - It singled out entities that could provide scalable access to downstream customers, sensitive networks, or strategic programs. It targeted endpoint management platforms, network management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators, and control plane technologies that play a crucial role within enterprise environments. Hundreds of victims have been identified across telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms, and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, and emergency services. Volt Typhoon (aka Bronze Silhouette, Insidious Taurus, UNC3236, Vanguard Panda, and Voltzite) is the moniker assigned to a China-linked state-sponsored group known for its targeting of critical infrastructure networks, particularly communications, energy, transportation, and water and wastewater systems sectors. Known to be active since at least 2021, the threat actor was previously observed exploiting a file upload vulnerability in Versa Director as a zero-day (CVE-2024-39717) to deliver a bespoke web shell called VersaMem designed to harvest credentials and enable access to downstream customers. The latest findings from Black Lotus Labs show that the security flaw was one among four confirmed zero-day campaigns the threat actor has conducted through Silent Train. The remaining three vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 - A set of insecure deserialization and command injection vulnerabilities in N-able N-central. CVE-2026-20127 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller CVE-2026-16812 - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator Separately, Volt Typhoon is also suspected to have taken advantage of a likely zero-day vulnerability in Quest KACE before it was patched in October 2025. The campaign is estimated to have impacted more than 30 victims. "Silent Train is built around rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise devices that are exploited on demand, used against carefully selected targets, cleaned up after each operation, and continuously refreshed," Black Lotus Labs said. "This model has enabled Volt Typhoon to conduct exploitation and post-exploitation operations with exceptional operational security while minimizing opportunities for detection, attribution, and disruption." A defining characteristic of these attacks is the repeated targeting of systems that can open the door to broad visibility, control, and access across large enterprise environments of strategic value to the U.S. What's interesting is that the covert access capability began to take shape sometime around November 2023, just weeks before the first round of disruption targeting KV-botnet, an IoT botnet linked to multiple China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors, including Volt Typhoon. Silent Train's operational activity is said to have surged in the wake of the botnet's second disruption in late January 2024, while simultaneously shifting to an ephemeral infrastructure comprising diverse device types and across geographies. "Rather than continue using persistent infrastructure, Volt Typhoon shifted to a model using one-time-use chains of compromised devices that it could rebuild as needed," Black Lotus Labs said. "Volt Typhoon rapidly assembled and dismantled transient infrastructure, creating a resilient, secure, and compartmentalized framework that protected valuable access." Described as a "layered, multi-hop framework," Silent Train is designed to let Volt Typhoon operators relay malicious traffic through several devices before it reaches the targets so as to obscure its origins from both victims and defenders. Each link in the chain serves a specific purpose - Virtual private servers (VPS) that function as a temporary staging area and allow threat actors to provision and discard them after each session. The sessions begin from VPS infrastructure located outside the U.S. Compromised non-U.S. SOHO and IoT devices located across different countries, providers, and hardware that conceal the starting point of the attack. U.S.-based compromised devices that function as an exit node before reaching the domestic victim and help evade geofencing and IP reputation blocklists. No less than 27 device classes, ranging from SOHO and IoT devices (e.g., TP-Link, Intelbras, Ruckus Wireless, SATO, NETGEAR, Zyxel, and Cambium) to enterprise platforms (e.g., Fortinet, Cisco, PRTG, Mirth Connect, and CyberPanel), have been exploited and enrolled into the covert network. "Silent Train stands out for its operational discipline, focusing on short-lived, selfmanaged sessions rather than persistent relays or C2 infrastructure," Black Lotus Labs said. "To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node." "This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and 'live off the land' utilities. At the end of operational sessions, they removed every artifact and dismantled the operational chain in their wake. Silent Train sessions lasted about four hours on average, with some lasting only minutes." Another notable aspect is the designation of certain device types to specific positions within Silent Train. For instance, Intelbras modems have been found to only appear as relay nodes, while Netgear Orbi and Fortinet FortiGate appliances served as U.S.-based intermediary and exit points responsible for interacting with the victim. Put differently, the infrastructure points to deliberate compartmentalization across layers, confining some device types to certain roles that remain constant while the underlying infrastructure itself changes over time so as to complicate attribution efforts. By early 2025, however, Silent Train is believed to have evolved from a completely ephemeral relay network to a hybrid architecture that retained enterprise-grade devices for an average of one to three months instead of changing them after each engagement. Subsequent maturation of the platform introduced reverse-tunnel variants that used open-source proxies like Chisel and FRP to send traffic from infected devices to upstream infrastructure. Within the U.S., Hawaii, California, and Texas have emerged as the focus areas of Silent Train operations, which boils down to the fact that these states host major military installations, telecommunications infrastructure, defense contractors, satellite communications providers, and critical logistics networks. "Victimology indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region," Black Lotus Labs said. "The resulting picture is one of a highly structured framework built to acquire, protect, and sustain strategic access at scale. Through repeated targeting of centralized management platforms and control plane technologies, Silent Train shows how Volt Typhoon systematically pursues and preserves access to some of the most consequential networks in the United States."

1un7aii.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 28, 2026Mobile Security / App Security Third-party Android app stores can now apply to Google for permission to install apps with one tap, without Android's usual confirmation screens, and to update them in the background. To qualify, a store must pass identity checks and send Google its full catalog, along with every new app and update, for ongoing malware scanning. Approved stores get the features from December 1, but only on devices running Android 17 QPR2 or later in supported countries, which do not include the US. Today, a user installing apps from a third-party store must first enable the store to install apps, then confirm each install and each update. From December 1, a store in Google's Registered App Stores program gets that permission automatically once it is approved, and its updates run in the background under the user's own update settings. Google announced the program in March, alongside changes it said resolved its disputes with Epic Games. Joining is optional, and stores that stay out will continue to operate as they do today. Under Google's rules, the store must still get the user's explicit consent for each install and "must not install apps silently without user consent." Large downloads and background installs must show a visible notification while they run. If an install is started on another device, the store must show a notification that does not close automatically. IT administrators can block registered stores from being installed on managed devices. Google's program pages do not say whether the block also applies to a store that is already installed. Beyond the catalog scanning, Google's requirements say a store must: be registered as an organization and keep its developer identity verified under Android developer verification, Google's identity check for app developers send every version of its own app to Google for malware screening, exactly matching the version it publishes on the web and through other channels work to keep malware and other potentially harmful apps out of its catalog fix major security flaws that come to its attention not block other app stores from being installed, interfere with them, or hide or change Android's security notifications pay a $10,000 yearly fee, due before Google starts its review Each store stays responsible and liable for everything in its catalog. Google won't moderate the content in registered stores. If more than 1% of install attempts or more than 2% of a store's apps are found to be potentially harmful over a 30-day period, Google charges additional fees to screen and clean up the catalog. A store that fails to meet any requirement, including paying on time, can be removed from the program until the issue is resolved. Google gives notice and a chance to fix it first. Google's program pages do not describe how submitted apps are scanned, how quickly new uploads are checked, or what results the checks produce. Registered stores also get a Google tool, the Android Developer ID API, to check whether each app in their catalog comes from a verified developer and can be installed. Google recommends that stores block installs of apps that fail the check. Android developer verification is a separate Google program, now in its first phase with seven app stores. Since September 30, certified Android devices in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand have checked that apps from those stores come from verified developers, according to Google. Google plans to extend the checks worldwide in 2027. Availability follows each user's home country. Short trips to unsupported countries do not turn off one-tap installs or automatic updates. Android 17 QPR2 is one of Android's quarterly platform releases (QPRs). Its latest version, released October 16, is still a beta, and Google's release notes give no date for the final release. In the US, a separate Google program for distributing third-party stores through Google Play has been in effect since July 22.

1jtq7xg.text: Sony Network Communications has confirmed a data breach that compromised approximately 2.5 million records containing current and former customers’ personal information. A Sony Group Corporation subsidiary, the company provides telecommunications and technology services, acting as an internet service provider (ISP) in Japan. The breach occurred on October 19 and was detected four days later, when the company shut down the compromised servers and blocked external communication. In an announcement yesterday, the company said that its So-net member database, supporting its internet access service, was accessed by an unauthorized party. The investigation confirmed that a total of 2,585,481 customer records had been exposed, including the following types of information: Full names Phone numbers Email addresses User IDs Dates of birth Gender Internet Connection IDs No banking, payment card, or other account details were exposed. An additional 54,401 email addresses from several email services were also exposed along with account passwords. The company advises users to change their passwords. In the breakdown of exposed records, Sony Network Communications says there are 2,141,986 So-net entries and 443,495 plala (S Course) records. The latter impacts another internet service provider, NTT Docomo, which contracts Sony Network Communications to provide its Docomo Hikari services. NTT Docomo also notified customers about the breach and warned of phishing emails and fake websites impersonating its d POINT Club and a Universal Studios Japan (USJ) campaign, falsely claiming that recipients had won and prompting them to enter personal information to claim tickets. Docomo says the incident affects all current Hikari service clients and those who canceled within the preceding six months. Sony reported the incident to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission and is investigating its cause and scope. As of October 27, neither company had confirmed misuse of the exposed data in the wild. Since the start of the year, multiple cyberattacks have targeted high-value companies and providers in Japan. One of the most recent is the incident at GMO Internet Group and its Onamae Desktop Cloud service, which suffered a widespread malware attack on customer servers. Telecommunications giant KDDI suffered a breach affecting 12 million customers, and IDC Frontier was targeted by ransomware. Previously, NTT was hit in early 2025 by hackers who gained access to its systems and stole the data of 18,000 corporate customers. The recent rate of data breaches is so unprecedented and threatening that the Japanese government held urgent meetings on Monday to plan its response. 165dh2v.text: A chain of logic flaws, with no memory corruption, can turn a malicious web page into code running on a Windows computer outside Microsoft Edge's sandbox, a security researcher has shown. Orange Tsai of DEVCORE published the full method on October 28, five months after the chain won $175,000 at the Pwn2Own Berlin contest in May. Microsoft fixed the Edge bugs the day after the contest, so an up-to-date browser is not at risk. A browser sandbox is the wall that keeps a web page's code inside the browser and off the rest of the computer. Breaking out of it, and then running a program, is what turns a web bug into full control of the machine. Browser escapes like this almost always rely on memory corruption. This one used none. In his write-up, Tsai describes a chain built solely from logic errors in how Edge and Windows handle ordinary features, and he says the whole exploit is under 100 lines of code. The result is a universal cross-site scripting (UXSS) primitive: a way to run JavaScript on any website, bypassing the content security policy meant to prevent it. Because the attack starts from the browser's own process, it can reach sites like google.com that an ordinary web bug cannot touch. Tsai calls this a new attack surface rather than a one-off bug. This was a competition exploit, not an attack seen in the wild. Tsai demonstrated it on stage at Pwn2Own; there is no evidence it has been used against real users, and the public CVE records list exploitation as none. One step in the chain restarts the browser, which Tsai notes is a convenience for the contest and not needed in a real attack. The chain begins with an Edge feature for business sign-ins called a conditional access navigation throttle. Tsai found that triggering it lets the browser's own process start a new navigation that is not tied to the page that asked for it, so Edge attaches it to whichever tab is open. That mismatch is the first bug, and it produces the UXSS. Making it run without a click took four more weaknesses. Edge checked that the request came from a trusted Microsoft site, but Tsai bypassed the check by opening the request from a second window. Edge's popup blocker should have stopped that window, but Edge carried a hardcoded list of allowed addresses, and one of them opened the popup. The attack also required the victim to be already signed in, which the Edge auto-sign-in feature provides on its own when the user visits a Microsoft site. Lastly, the chain reads the victim's email address from a Microsoft site, assets.msn.com, which returned it to any website due to a misconfigured cross-origin setting. Running JavaScript everywhere is still not in control of the computer. To escape the sandbox, Tsai used Edge's reading mode, Immersive Reader, which runs under a custom read:// address that Microsoft left off the list of pages barred from running scripts. From there, the chain called an internal Edge function meant to zip up diagnostic logs and abused it to write a file with an attacker-chosen name and content anywhere on disk. That file write is turned into code execution in two steps. The chain overwrites a configuration file that controls which websites may launch which protocol handlers, then restarts Edge so the file is read. It then launches a telnet:// link; because Windows does not ship a telnet program by default, it searches the system path for one and runs an attacker-planted copy from a folder the low-privileged user can write to. Microsoft shipped the fix on May 15, the day after the contest, in Edge Stable version 148.0.3967.70. That release carried three Edge-specific fixes, tracked as CVE-2026-45492, CVE-2026-45494, and CVE-2026-45495. The first is recorded as a security feature bypass, and the second as a spoofing bug, both affecting Edge versions before 148.0.3967.70. Microsoft's records rate the first two at 5.4 on a 10-point scale, a medium score that reflects a single bug in isolation, not the full chain that strings them into code execution. DEVCORE said the fix came within 24 hours of the disclosure. Updating Edge closes this chain. Because the fix shipped in May, a browser on automatic updates has long since received it, and no separate action is needed. Tsai built the chain by hand, over about two months, without any AI help, and frames the work as a point about where human research still matters. "The hard part is finding them, and once you find them all, chaining is the easiest part," he writes of the logic bugs. The research won the 2026 Pwnie Award for Epic Achievement.

ukbasq.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Espionage Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what appears to be an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted attack orchestrated by a suspected China-nexus threat actor that has leveraged the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to breach exposed systems. The activity, which was observed on October 25, 2026, involved an attacker combining PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including three systems in a U.S. government-affiliated environment. "The affected devices run specific versions of a large vendor's firewall software," cybersecurity firm Dream said. "The attacker then launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration." The name of the affected vendor was not disclosed, but the Israeli company said it notified the entity. The attack chain essentially brings together two sets of vulnerabilities impacting PHP and the Linux kernel - PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2) that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution Fragnesia, a Linux kernel local privilege escalation vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-46300 (CVSS score: 7.8) "The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell," Dream researchers explained. "It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform." "The vulnerability targets PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the firewall's appweb management server. The firewall OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack." The custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain, coupled with CVE-2026-46300, is said to have rooted 25 servers across the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Artifacts discovered by Dream indicate that the operation started with exploit development in a lab environment before obtaining persistent access to a U.S. government organization's internal Active Directory domain. "Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a U.S. government-affiliated environment," the company noted. The links to AI-assisted tooling stem from evidence pointing to the installation of Anthropic's Claude Code in the attack infrastructure, along with the presence of API keys for FOFA and an AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan configured with large language models (LLMs) from DeepSeek and Kimi. What's more, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across nearly 40 scripts suggest the use of AI to augment the development process. The entire operation, per Dream, unfolds as follows - Attacker uses FOFA to identify approximately 19,000 internet-facing firewalls with exposed management interfaces worldwide. A custom version scanner is executed to determine which among those devices are online and what operating system version they are running. About 5,000 devices respond with the version information. The attacker filters the servers to those located in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and then limits the scope to systems that match newer release branches running PHP 8.0.30. This step yields 240 targets. The target list is fed as input to an automated batch runner that exploits the PHP2Shell-Fragnesia chain, plants a PHP web shell on a publicly accessible directory on the firewall, verifies root access, and logs the target's hostname and IP to a CSV file. This step allows the attacker to gain root access to 24 servers. Two of the successfully compromised systems are identified as belonging to a U.S. government-affiliated organization. One of them crashes shortly after it was rooted on October 23, 2026, at 6:14 p.m. UTC and never comes back online. The attacker carries out a dedicated campaign to successfully root a second system on October 24, 2026, at 10:09 a.m. UTC. The attacker exploits the second system to build a persistent channel into the internal network via a reverse SSH tunnel connecting the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure. At 11:35 a.m. UTC, a third government server is compromised using the same method, the only difference being that this was an internal firewall management server only reachable through the tunnel. The total number of rooted servers reaches 25. The attacker targets Active Directory to decrypt the LDAP service account password, enumerate users, and spray passwords against every user account using organization-themed passwords in an attempt to extract credentials. The operation also attempts to create backdoor Active Directory accounts. It's unclear if the activity allowed the threat actor to successfully find valid credentials or create backdoor accounts. As a result, the full extent of the compromise remains indeterminate. "Since [the] U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts," Dream said. "The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization's identity infrastructure. The 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked with active web shells. The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running. And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional OS versions." The disclosure comes as the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities have witnessed only limited exploitation in the wild, with threat actors highlighting the challenges in converting a proof-of-concept (PoC) into a reliable attack vector against real targets despite integrating them into their campaigns. "In practice it's unexploitable crap. To exploit real targets you need the offsets from libphp.so, which are unique to every build and impossible to brute-force. You can reproduce it on your own test bench, or if you already have access to the target's file system," a member who goes by the handle c0d3x on the XSS forum said, according to Flare.

1maddko.text: Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including for zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems. The framework has been dubbed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation, and refreshes it continuously. Researchers at Black Lotus Labs, the threat research division of communications company Lumen, have been tracking Silent Train for three years and confirmed that Volt Typhoon exploited at least four zero-day vulnerabilities in attacks targeting edge and management infrastructure. Targets include telecommunication firms, government agencies, defense contractors, educational institutes, utilities/critical infrastructure, satellite service providers, IT firms, MSPs, transportation, aviation, and emergency services. Black Lotus Labs’ observations indicate the most targeted regions are California, Texas, and Hawaii, suggesting a focus on Indo-Pacific matters. Victims map Source: Black Lotus Labs Volt Typhoon previously targeted U.S. critical infrastructure, including communications, energy, transportation, and water systems, with CISA warning that it seeks to establish access for potential disruption during a future crisis or conflict. According to the researchers, Silent Train's deployment was partly fueled by the FBI's disruption of KV-Botnet, a botnet that Volt Typhoon used to evade detection when attacking critical infrastructure in the US. Activity comparison over time Source: Black Lotus Labs Silent Train relay network Silent Train is practically a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices that Volt Typhoon uses to hide the origin of its attacks. The operators route their activity through VPS infrastructure outside the United States, then pass it through hacked devices such as routers that act as intermediate relays before launching attacks. Black Lotus Labs says Intelbras modems served as overseas relays, while Netgear Orbi devices acted as hops in the U.S. Silent Train attack overview Source: Black Lotus Labs The threat actor's use of Silent Train involves exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, exfiltrating data, and maintaining persistent remote access to compromised systems. By monitoring Silent Train activity, the researchers were able to observe zero-day exploits for the following products: CVE-2026-16812 – VeloCloudOrchestrator CVE-2026-20127 – Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 – N-able N-central CVE-2024-39717 – Versa Director Quest KACE (suspected zero-day) Compromising these platforms gives threat actors broad administrative control, enabling credential theft, remote access, and reach into downstream customers without the “noisy” lateral movement that might trigger detection. Exploitation timeline Source: Black Lotus Labs “To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node,” Black Lotus Labs explains in a report today. “This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and “live off the land” utilities.” After the session ends, typically in under 8 hours, the threat actors remove all their tooling, keys, and configuration files from the disposable relays. By early 2025, researchers noticed that the framework become hybrid, using disposable relays alongside compromised enterprise systems thaat were retained between one and three months. Black Lotus Labs believes Silent Train was reserved for high-value targets and careful, hands-on operations conducted on China Standard Time (CST) timezone. The use of zero-days against those targets further strengthens the assumption. The researchers recommend strengthening security around centralized management systems, restricting internet access to administrative interfaces, rapidly patching vulnerabilities, and centralizing logs with longer retention. They also advise monitoring for unusual administrative activity, reviewing trusted connections that could expose customer or partner networks, and following CISA and NCSC guidance on Volt Typhoon. cubjns.text: Microsoft again asked Entra ID administrators to migrate users to phishing-resistant methods to avoid sign-in disruptions before it retires SMS and voice authentication in February 2027. This retirement process applies only to Microsoft Entra ID workforce tenant authentication scenarios and not to Azure AD B2C or Microsoft Entra External ID customer identity scenarios. Before Microsoft retires SMS and voice authentication, admins should ensure all users in their organizations use a phishing-resistant method, since they will no longer be able to use them to complete multifactor authentication and log in to their accounts. Admins can choose from passkeys, QR code authentication, FIDO2 security keys, and other Entra ID-supported sign-in methods. "Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication will retire starting February 1, 2027. Complete your migration before rollout begins to avoid interrupting users' sign-in experience," Microsoft said in a Microsoft 365 Message Center update on Tuesday. "SMS and voice are vulnerable to phishing and SIM-swap attacks. Microsoft recommends passkeys for stronger, phishing-resistant protection. You can also migrate to another supported authentication method or retain SMS and voice by configuring a customer-managed telecom provider (CYOT) through the Microsoft Security Store." As Microsoft noted in a previous reminder issued in September, admins with the Authentication Policy Administrator, Global Reader, or Security Reader roles can find users with SMS or voice authentication with the Entra SMS/Voice Policy Scanner PowerShell script. Organizations that must use phone-based authentication have to configure third-party telecom providers through the Microsoft Security Store. Passkeys now the default Entra ID auth method In July, Microsoft announced that passkeys will start rolling out as the default authentication experience for the Entra ID enterprise identity service starting in September. "As the rollout reaches each organization, users enabled for SMS or voice authentication will automatically be enabled for passkeys, and the next time they perform multifactor authentication, they'll be prompted to register a passkey," Microsoft said. "Following this transition, on February 1, 2027, Microsoft will retire Microsoft-provided telecom delivery for SMS and voice authentication and will no longer offer SMS and voice as a native Microsoft Entra capability." Microsoft also retired SMS first-factor sign-in for Microsoft Entra ID Free tenants in August due to phishing, fraud, and account compromise risks, and stopped enabling it for newly created tenants. Detailed guidance on deploying and managing phishing-resistant passwordless authentication in Entra ID is available on this dedicated Microsoft documentation page. 6um3wx.text: Attackers are actively exploiting vulnerabilities across critical network infrastructure, and PHP flaws known as "PHP2Shell" put the web management interfaces of firewalls, VPNs, application delivery controllers, and other appliances at risk. The findings come from Eclypsium's October InfraTrust Pulse, a monthly report tracking security advisories affecting network devices, servers, firmware, chips, and other infrastructure. Between September 18 and October 14, InfraTrust tracked 133 new security advisories across 18 vendors, covering 2,813 vulnerabilities. Of those advisories, 37 were rated critical, five had a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and 58 could be exploited remotely without authentication. Sixteen newly published advisories included vulnerabilities listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (KEV) as they were actively exploited. The report also warns that many network appliances, including firewalls, VPN gateways, application delivery controllers, and network-attached storage devices, embed PHP into their management interfaces. Because vendors compile PHP into appliance firmware, customers commonly cannot install the recent PHP security updates themselves and must instead wait for each vendor to release updated firmware. InfraTrust therefore recommends that administrators make sure PHP-backed management interfaces are not exposed to the Internet while waiting for PHP2Shell patches. Critical infrastructure under attack Some of the most serious vulnerabilities affect systems at the edge of enterprise networks or used to manage other infrastructure. Threat actors target these devices because they can provide initial access to corporate environments or serve as a springboard for further attacks. Among the actively exploited flaws highlighted by InfraTrust are: Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 were disclosed on September 27 after attacks had already been observed against unpatched appliances. A separate NetScaler flaw, CVE-2026-88779, affecting appliances configured for SAML was also later added to CISA's KEV catalog after exploitation was detected. Ivanti Connect Secure: CVE-2026-104935 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands on vulnerable VPN gateways. Ivanti said it had exploited a limited number of customers when it published the advisory. CISA later added it to the KEV. Check Point Security Management Server: CVE-2026-93616 allows an unauthenticated attacker to upload and execute scripts on management and logging systems. Check Point Research observed targeted attacks exploiting the flaw on September 12, targeting Spark customers. Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: CVE-2026-76504 allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and gain administrator access to the management API. Cisco became aware of active exploitation in September. Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: CVE-2026-93952 is a maximum-severity flaw affecting the system used to configure SD-WAN Edge devices. Arista says it is being actively exploited and later disclosed a second, separate exploited vulnerability (CVE-2026-114625) in the same product on October 22. FortiMail: CVE-2026-104286 is a critical path traversal flaw that allows an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files through the web interface. Fortinet confirmed it was exploited in attacks. Cisco Secure Email Gateway: CVE-2026-76519 can allow a malicious email attachment to lead to arbitrary file writes and command execution as root on vulnerable systems. Cisco learned of exploitation in October. F5 BIG-IP APM: CVE-2026-94127 is a critical heap overflow that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on systems configured as OAuth authorization servers. F5 says the vulnerability has been exploited. PAN-OS management interface: Palo Alto Networks reported exploitation of CVE-2026-0322 in attacks on firewalls, allowing an authenticated administrator with network access to execute code as root. php2shell exposes another problem InfraTrust also warns that the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities expose another weakness in network infrastructure, as many appliances embed PHP directly into their management interfaces. The two PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, allow unauthenticated remote code execution, and the PHP project fixed them on October 21. While most focus on these vulnerabilities has been on websites and web applications written in PHP, PHP is also used for management interfaces of firewalls, application delivery controllers, VPN appliances, and network-attached storage devices. For impacted devices, administrators usually cannot update PHP themselves because vendors compile it directly into the appliance firmware. Instead, customers must wait for each vendor to rebuild and release updated firmware or software containing the patched PHP version. Soon after the disclosure, Palo Alto Networks, F5, NetScaler, Check Point, and QNAP confirmed that some of their products were affected, while they still developed fixes for appliances. The report also highlights a similar issue in other software components that infrastructure vendors bundle into their products. CVE-2026-31431, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw known as Copy Fail, has now appeared in 29 advisories across eight vendors, up from 19 advisories from six vendors last month. InfraTrust also found older, exploited vulnerabilities in bundled components, including an Android kernel flaw affecting HP LaserJet Enterprise printers and a 2020 jQuery vulnerability in Dell Data Lakehouse software. InfraTrust recommends that administrators prioritize patching NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure because these remote-access gateways can serve as a doorway into corporate networks. Next, it recommends Fortinet's October 22 FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer security updates for internet-facing devices. The report then recommends focusing on Check Point Security Management Server, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, VeloCloud Orchestrator, FortiMail, Cisco Secure Email Gateway, affected BIG-IP APM systems, and PAN-OS management interfaces. ch7gpu.text: Here's a prediction: we're about to see a stellar quarter for application security companies. PHP2Shell is about to become the strongest budget argument application security vendors have had in years. AI helped researchers find two remote code execution vulnerabilities in the language behind 69% of the web, attackers targeted it before the patch shipped, and the pitch writes itself: find more bugs and fix them faster. Enterprises should rethink this idea. Security teams cannot patch at machine speed, but they can reduce what an attacker can reach after exploitation by focusing on identity as the control plane.
