Systems). 🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars From Zero-Days to Exploits in Minutes: Are You Ready for AI Threats? → AI-powered cyberattacks are accelerating, shrinking the time security teams have to detect, investigate, and respond. Are your defenses ready to keep up? Join this expert-led webinar to discover how to strengthen AI threat readiness, improve attack-surface visibility, and build faster, more resilient security operations before attackers gain the upper hand. Learn How to Turn Identity Context Into Faster, Smarter SOC Response → Your security tools can detect suspicious activity, but without identity context, critical threats may go unnoticed. As machine identities and AI agents expand the attack surface, SOC teams need deeper visibility to respond effectively. Join this expert-led webinar to discover how connecting identity intelligence with security operations can help uncover hidden risks, accelerate investigations, and contain threats faster. 📰 Around the Cyber World CrowdStrike said it uncovered four previously unreported threat actors orchestrating campaigns in which Claude Code is used to make decisions and execute commands, demonstrating how agentic AI is commoditizing baseline offensive cyber operations. This includes a Spanish/English-speaking operator that has compromised at least 15 Argentina-based healthcare entities and exfiltrated credentials and medical records from at least one victim; a Chinese-speaking operator that breached government entities of two countries and targeted private sector entities in Brazil and the U.S.; an Indonesian-speaking actor using 819 skills to break into Indonesian government domains and several private-sector entities; and group of Russian-speaking individuals who have exfiltrated corporate client data from a U.S.-based customer relationship management vendor and compromised several private-sector SaaS and data center entities based in Russia, Kyrgyzstan, and the U.S. Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center is alerting 3,182 patients their personal health information may have been exposed after a staff member uploaded a spreadsheet of patient information to an outside AI platform that was not approved for use. The information included patients admitted and treated between May 2026 and September 2026, including their names, dates of admission and treatment, medical record numbers, account numbers, the department that treated them, medications given, and the names of their providers. The U.S.-based hospital said it reached out to the AI platform provider to delete the data. Anthropic said it used Claude to analyze 25 major open-source projects written in C, C++, Java, PHP, and Python, and found 493 issues. This included a configuration flaw that sat undetected in unspecified software for 21 years. In a separate report, Anthropic said large language models (LLMs) are making "formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale," allowing code to be translated into a mathematical model and prove that it "always follows some defined set of security rules." The AI company said frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. The developer of the MeshCentral remote access software is urging users to update to version 1.3.1. "The[re] is an active exploit/hacker attacking MeshCentral servers and taking control of it and remote clients," the developer said. Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit CVE-2026-25243, a heap memory-corruption bug in Redis's RESTORE command, beginning around October 16. "One source hit the decoy five times on a timer with an identical payload: fingerprint the server, shape the heap with 26 key writes, fire a single malformed-zipmap RESTORE that triggers the documented over-read, run a throwaway Lua compute probe, then FLUSHALL the keyspace, destroying data and its own artifacts every run. Note that the bug needs command access to be exploitable," Defused Cyber said. Security researcher Patrick Wardle has detailed Heartbreaker, a Rust-based macOS ransomware sample that was uploaded to VirusTotal in May 2025. The malware attempts to set up a LaunchAgent for persistence, and then encrypts files in the user's Downloads folder. "Heartbreaker is unlikely to pose a major real-world threat in its current form," Wardle said. "It only targets files under ~/Downloads, lacks awareness of macOS privacy protections, embeds a universal recovery key, depends on a now-unavailable build framework, and performs an exceptionally noisy Rust installation and compilation workflow. Its disabled 'Decrypt Files' button does not actually recover anything, either. Heartbreaker demonstrates an unusual approach to metamorphism on macOS. Rather than decrypting or rewriting its machine code in memory, it carries its own Rust source, transforms that source, invokes the native build toolchain, and attempts to replace itself with the result. Because each generation embeds its newly transformed source, the design can – in principle – continue across executions." Axios reported that major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some attempting actions that appear independent of user instructions. Although the agents log in with the user's permission and credentials, the problem lies in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot. "Some banks have tracked activity when agents — programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf — contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions," Axios reported. Banks are responding to the threat by either restricting them or allowing read-only access. In a new attack, Forever Security said it caught a malicious AGENTS.md markdown instructions file in a customer's Downloads folder that tricked an AI coding agent into installing a rogue npm package named "function-color," which was identified as part of a software supply chain attack campaign codenamed MALFEX. "An AGENTS.md is a file a coding agent is built to trust and obey, and ~/Downloads is the one folder a website can drop a file into with no click and no permission," Forever Security said. "Together, that lets the web plant orders your own agent carries out. Markdown is the new executable. The planted file makes the agent rewrite its own configuration. From there it can install malware (remote code execution) or hand over its own login token (account takeover)." It's unclear how the malicious instructions file ended up on the target's Downloads folder, although it's possible that threat actors could trick a user into downloading it by simply visiting a specially crafted page. A sophisticated organized crime gang is said to have hacked into Staples, issued millions of dollars' worth of gift cards, and gone on a spending spree across the U.S., 404 Media reported. In October 2025, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 detailed a threat cluster dubbed Jingle Thief that targeted cloud environments associated with organizations in the retail and consumer services sectors for gift card fraud. Pseudonymous blockchain investigator ZachXBT (aka Zachary Wolk) has revealed that a Chinese organized crime syndicate laundered more than $1 billion stolen in multiple cryptocurrency exploits for North Korea's Lazarus Group. ZachXBT said he posed as a paying client to infiltrate the money laundering network in February 2025, in the days following the massive Bybit hack, leading to the identification of a cluster of more than $12 million in Bybit-linked funds. About 442,000 USDT linked to the cluster was later frozen by Tether. Federal investigators suspect that at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm helped operate Shinywire, a now-defunct ShinyHunters site used to pressure nearly 100 hacked organizations into paying, according to security journalist Brian Krebs. Signal messages that authorities accessed when they apprehended ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap in the Netherlands reportedly show frequent contact with Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky and at least one executive at a U.S. consulting firm, who sometimes knew about new victims before the victims themselves, citing an unnamed source. "The Dutch hacker's chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files," Krebs said. The U.S. Army is allegedly developing a program to deploy autonomous AI agents that can navigate digital and network infrastructures of its adversaries, and "neutralize" them, The Intercept reported. The nascent program, codenamed ECHOTRIBBLE, is primarily focused on offensive missions with the goal of "disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target." In addition, the system "would function almost like a computer worm, silently navigating a foreign network and hopping from device to device until it finds the Army's quarry, hitting targets in the cloud as well as those on “air-gapped” systems that are disconnected from networks entirely. Once its task is complete, ECHOTRIBBLE's agents would effectively self-destruct, ideally without having been noticed by the target at all." A group of academics from the University of British Columbia have detailed ICS-Sniper, a proof-of-concept attack aimed at industrial facilities that rely on cloud-hosted SCADA systems. It's described as a "targeted blackhole attack that analyzes the VPN traffic metadata (sizes, direction, timing of packets) to identify narrow time windows, called critical superperiods, during which the site-SCADA traffic would likely contain highly critical commands or data." An attacker with control over a router on the network path could examine the size, direction, and timing of VPN-encrypted packets to predict when critical commands or data are likely to be exchanged, and then deliver malicious payloads during those time periods. "Post-analysis, in a subsequent operational cycle, ICS-Sniper drops a small set of payload-carrying packets in the critical superperiods to disrupt the ICS's operations," the study said. In tests on emulated versions of a Secure Water Treatment (SWaT) plant testbed, the attack delayed the start of clean water pumping by about 15 minutes and kept a valve open more than nine minutes longer than intended. A new Windows malware called SiriusQT offers various capabilities in a single package: remote access, HVNC, browser automation, credential theft, cryptocurrency wallet collection, clipboard monitoring, keylogging, process injection, persistence, anti-analysis checks, and custom encrypted command-and-control traffic. SiriusQT has been advertised by a seller named GhostKernel on dark web forums since April 2026. Its author is Amonus. At least 30 users bought a valid license, Group-IB said. A lifetime subscription costs $500, but cracked versions of the program are said to be shared by multiple actors. Campaigns using the malware have targeted the U.K., Germany, France, Spain, Italy, and the Netherlands. GhostKernel has also been observed advertising BTMob v4.0, an Android trojan, on their Telegram channel. As many as 2,894 ransomware attacks have been recorded in Q3 2026, a nearly 50% jump from more than a year ago, led by The Gentlemen (383) and Qilin (363). "Both break in through stolen credentials and exposed VPNs, and both hit many of the same industries," Nord Security said. […]

iaza16.text: Two critical flaws in Wasmtime, a WebAssembly runtime that can be built into other software, could allow a malicious WebAssembly module to escape the sandbox intended to contain it, the project's maintainers say. An attacker would first need a vulnerable Wasmtime build to compile a module they control, and one of the flaws affects only ARM64 systems. Fixed versions were released on October 19 and 20, and the maintainers have not reported any attacks. Wasmtime runs WebAssembly code outside web browsers. Both bugs are in Cranelift, the compiler it uses by default to turn WebAssembly into machine code. Wasmtime's maintainers at the Bytecode Alliance rated each flaw 9.9 out of 10 on the CVSS scale in advisories published on October 19. CVE-2026-115889 affects Wasmtime across all processor architectures. CVE-2026-115893 affects only ARM64, also called aarch64. The sandbox is meant to keep a module inside set limits. A module can only use its own memory and the host functions it is given, and its code can only jump to checked locations. Because both flaws need a module the attacker controls, the risk is highest for services that compile modules written by other people. Fastly, for example, says its Compute platform runs customer code using Wasmtime. The advisories do not name any affected services or specify what an attacker could access after escaping the sandbox. Neither flaw was in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as of October 26. Which Versions Are Affected The two flaws were fixed at different times, so whether your version is affected depends on your release line and, for one flaw, your processor architecture. Wasmtime version CVE-2026-115889 (any architecture) CVE-2026-115893 (ARM64 only) What to do Before 36.0.19 (includes 24.x) Affected Affected Update to 36.0.19, or move to 48.0.7, 49.0.4 or 50.0.0 36.0.19 Fixed Fixed None needed for these flaws 37.0.0 through 42.x Affected Affected Move to 48.0.7, 49.0.4 or 50.0.0 43.0.0 through 47.x Not affected Affected Move to 48.0.7, 49.0.4 or 50.0.0 48.0.0 through 48.0.6 Not affected Affected Update to 48.0.7 48.0.7 Not affected Fixed None needed for these flaws 49.0.0 through 49.0.3 Not affected Affected Update to 49.0.4 49.0.4, and 50.0.0 or later Not affected Fixed None needed for these flaws Wasmtime supports long-term support (LTS) releases, which are numbered in multiples of 12, for two years. Other releases get two months. Security fixes are guaranteed for supported releases. Only the 36, 48, 49, and 50 release lines are still supported. Every other line, including the 24.x LTS line whose support ended on August 20, 2026, got no fix. ARM64 hosts that updated to 36.0.7, 42.0.2, or 43.0.1 in April to fix an earlier Cranelift sandbox escape on ARM64 are still affected by CVE-2026-115893. What to Do Update to the fixed release for your line: 36.0.19, 48.0.7, or 49.0.4. Wasmtime 50.0.0, released on October 20, is fixed for both flaws. Hosts on an unsupported line need to move to one of these releases. Wasmtime can be built into other programs as a library, so updating the command-line tool does not fix them. Each program that includes Wasmtime needs to be rebuilt with a fixed version. Neither advisory lists a workaround. Until a host is updated, the risk comes from any module an outsider can supply. Both flaws are listed in RustSec, the database the cargo-audit tool uses to check Cargo.lock files, as RUSTSEC-2026-0380 and RUSTSEC-2026-0379. As of October 26, GitHub's advisory database had a reviewed entry for CVE-2026-115889 but none for CVE-2026-115893. GitHub says only reviewed entries trigger Dependabot alerts, so Dependabot users should not expect an alert for the ARM64 flaw. Spin, an open-source tool for building serverless WebAssembly apps that runs on Wasmtime, moved to Wasmtime 50.0.0 in version 4.2.4 on October 21. How the Two Flaws Work CVE-2026-115889 comes from how Cranelift stored the numbers it uses to track values inside a function. Before version 43, it packed these numbers into 24-bit fields, and in release builds, a number too large for its field overflowed without any error. Cranelift could then refer to the wrong value, producing incorrect machine code. A very large WebAssembly function, or one crafted to use many values, can use this to force type confusion and escape the sandbox, according to the advisory. Wasmtime's main development line had already removed the problem. A change merged on February 18 widened the fields to 32 bits and shipped in Wasmtime 43.0.0 on March 20. Its description presented it as a way to compile larger functions and did not mention security. The 36.x LTS line got the same change on October 19. The advisory does not say when the security impact was recognized. CVE-2026-115893 involves br_table, a WebAssembly instruction that jumps to one of many places in the code based on an index. An index outside the table goes to a default target. On ARM64, Cranelift sent these out-of-range indexes to the default with a branch that can only reach about 1 MiB. A br_table with more than about 256,000 targets made the jump table too big for that reach, so the branch silently pointed to the wrong place. Any Wasmtime engine on ARM64 with default settings "can be forced to jump to arbitrary code by a user-controlled Wasm module," the advisory says. The bug has been present since Wasmtime first supported ARM64 in 2020. The fix sends out-of-range indexes through the jump table itself, so no long branch is needed. Fixed versions also refuse to compile a br_table with more than 65,520 targets.

1nzpm62.text: Every SOC struggles with a pile of alerts. Very few of those alerts explain how an attack started or how it progressed. Network data, like that from a network detection and response (NDR) platform, connects individual alerts into one timeline, and it feeds the defensive systems that can tie all events together into one coordinated view. SOC teams often first see the shape of an intrusion through a series of smaller alerts that are triggered (e.g., when a signature matches a known malware hash, a threshold flags an unusual spike in failed logins, or an endpoint agent detects suspicious activity). When viewed through the SIEM dashboard, an attack often begins as a series of distinct events with related or overlapping timestamps. Artificial intelligence has accelerated modern attacks, enabling attackers to automate reconnaissance, craft targeted payloads, and execute scripts in seconds. Yet, speed does not obfuscate the need for stealth. To evade detection, adversaries deliberately draw out operations, hide inside standard admin tooling, and work in the quiet intervals between alarms. Adversaries might spend days or weeks inside an enterprise environment before an action generates a high-priority security alert. When an alert finally surfaces, it doesn’t necessarily mark the start of a compromise. It may, in fact, be one event in a much longer sequence. Analysts who investigate only the triggering event may miss the chained activity that explains how the intrusion developed. The anatomy of silent progression Between initial access and a high-severity alert, adversary activity can blend into ordinary business operations. Adversaries understand the operational limits of security teams, and they exploit them; if every DNS query, LDAP request, SMB connection, or authentication attempt generated an investigation, SOC queues would quickly become (even more) unmanageable. Tradecraft purposely takes advantage of that reality. Adversaries can spread reconnaissance across hours or distributed sources. Instead of launching an obvious scan, they may use a compromised account to query a domain controller over LDAP at a modest pace to map users, groups, and systems. A handful of Kerberos service ticket requests can yield credentials to crack offline, well outside the SOC’s view. Valid credentials then open the door to SMB or RDP, the same services administrators rely on every day, and the attacker moves from host to host. Files may be gathered on one internal system and compressed. Later, that system may reach an external destination over HTTPS or DNS at regular intervals, with just enough variation in timing to resemble normal traffic as it exfiltrates data. Each step borrows something the business already depends on. While individual actions may not necessarily look suspicious, their significance often emerges from relationships and sequences. For instance, a host that communicates with a new system once may be unremarkable. A host that queries several internal services, authenticates to a peer, establishes an SMB session, and then connects to an external destination presents a different investigative picture. The activity becomes more meaningful when viewed across time. When siloed tools see only slices of this type of transaction, they might miss the bigger picture. Context only becomes readily apparent when activities and signals are combined and correlated via network observation. What’s more, attackers increasingly use AI to automate reconnaissance and move faster. Defenders need to apply AI to the same problem, but it needs detailed network evidence from an NDR to search. The evidence between the alerts SecOps teams don’t have to turn detection thresholds down and drown analysts in more alerts just to spot adversary activity. Doing so would be untenable anyway. A SOC can’t investigate every DNS query, authentication request, or connection as though it were an incident. In addition, many teams operate with tools that show an alert fired yet offer sparse detail on how the activity behind it unfolded. To prevent blindspots, SOC teams can retain the underlying network telemetry so an analyst can go back and review what happened when an alert, outage, or other signal gives them a reason to look. However, that requires more than knowing when two systems exchanged traffic. Protocol-aware network data from an NDR platform can show the kind of interaction that took place, who or what participated, when it happened, and how that relationship evolved over time. For instance, if a workstation triggers an endpoint alert at 2:14 p.m. the alert may show an analyst what happened on the endpoint at that moment. Network evidence from an NDR can extend the timeline and answer a few crucial questions: Was the workstation querying an unusual domain earlier that day? Did it authenticate to another system or establish SMB connections to internal peers? Did those systems communicate with additional hosts? Did the workstation later establish an encrypted session with an external destination? Each individual event may have perfectly legitimate explanations. It’s only in combination, though, that the sequence provides a different level of context. For an investigator, that context helps establish whether the endpoint event was an isolated problem or one discrete stage in a broader progression. For an AI-assisted investigation, the context derived from NDR provides the evidence needed to search for related activity across hosts, users, protocols, and time rather than treating each alert as a separate event. Why this matters for the AI SOC AI in the SOC changes the economics of an investigation. While a human analyst has to decide which systems, users, sessions, and time periods deserve attention, an AI-assisted SOC can search across that same breadth of evidence much faster, bringing relevant data into one view in minutes rather than hours. Correlation and analysis can happen asynchronously, allowing analysts to review and query a broader set of data much sooner. When AI handles the synthesis, the process of identifying patterns is faster, still. When an attacker is patient, methodically timing actions across longer periods, evidence might be spread across hundreds of seemingly ordinary transactions. Since a human analyst can’t reasonably manually investigate each piece of evidence, the more practical approach is to construct an automated workflow in an NDR platform to identify context and look for relationships, then give the analyst the evidence so they can make a judgement call. The outcome is more activity examined, across more systems, over a longer period. The benefits are: Time savings: manual work is significantly reduced Clearer insights: more context can be surfaced by advanced algorithms searching across thousands of data points Better decisions: analysts can focus on making strategic risk decisions instead of picking apart pieces of alerts The same process can help with operational issues. If an application goes down, for example, network telemetry will show which services were communicating, where communications began to fail, which dependencies were affected, and what changed around the event. If the cause turns out to be malicious, the investigation already has a record of the activity. Beyond individual alerts Alerts give analysts a place to start an investigation. They do not necessarily explain what happened before it, what happened after it, what’s happening simultaneously, or whether other activity in the environment is related. Issues that appear routine in isolation may look very different when data is correlated and context is added. Network telemetry provides the surrounding evidence needed to build critical context. Protocol-aware data from the NDR preserves the details of network interactions, including both ends of a communication, the protocols and services involved, timestamps for those interactions, and how interactions change over time. It’s the telemetry that gives automated investigation workflows a broader body of evidence to work from when triaging a high-priority alert. With evidence available for automated analysis, AI agents can correlate activity over time, connect communications between systems, and surface sequences that would otherwise remain separate innocuous-looking events. The ability to apply context across disparate communications and sequences is what allows SOC teams to find the riskiest activity. Without this evidence, individual alerts and sequences may continue to present as harmless. Attackers have already identified the opportunity; now it’s time for defenders to apply the same principles and keep up. About Corelight: Your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions. Learn more about Corelight at https://corelight.com/cp/elitedefense

yx760k.text: A rentable Android spyware kit called uCreator takes over Telegram and WeChat accounts by hiding its code inside working copies of the two apps, researcher Ovi found. It only reaches people who install one of these tampered copies, spread outside the official app stores, or who run WeChat inside the kit makers' own container app. The kit's Telegram part matches Baohuo, a backdoor that Doctor Web reported in October 2025. Doctor Web found Baohuo in tampered copies of Telegram X, an Android app from Telegram. At the time, the company estimated that more than 58,000 devices were infected. The Hacker News compared the two reports. Doctor Web's technical description of Baohuo lists the same code namespace, com.ucreator.tgjar, the same command-and-control (C2) server, and matching command names as Ovi's analysis. Ovi's analysis, published October 21, 2026, does not mention Doctor Web's findings, and Doctor Web did not name the kit. It is not clear whether the kit's makers or one of their customers ran the campaign Doctor Web tracked. Who Is Exposed The tampered apps spread through sideloading, where a person installs an app file directly instead of from an app store, and through social engineering, Ovi found. He could not confirm how every victim was infected. A second route is the kit makers' own container app, called 洋葱盒子 ("Onion Box"), which runs other apps inside itself. Some of the tampered Telegram X copies use the same package name as the real app on Google Play, so the name alone does not give them away. Doctor Web found that Baohuo copies had been spreading since mid-2024 through in-app ads that led to fake app store sites. Those sites promoted Telegram X as a dating and video chat app. The sites' banners were available only in Portuguese, for users in Brazil, and in Indonesian. Even so, Doctor Web's 2025 map of infected devices by country put India first, at 22.8%, ahead of Brazil at 20.5% and Indonesia at 9.6%. Baohuo copies also turned up in the third-party stores APKPure, ApkSum and AndroidP. On APKPure, one was listed under the official developer's name, although its digital signature was different. Ovi got access to one of the kit's command servers. It held data on victims apparently located in China and the United States, but not enough for a reliable count. He calls his report "an analysis of technical capability, not a measurement of victim impact." The apparent targets, still unconfirmed, are users of mobile wallets and messaging apps in China and Southeast Asia, including WeCom, QQ, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, GCash and MoMo. He found code supporting about 20 apps, but has published code only for Telegram and WeChat. The kit's hooking engine is the part that lets its code intercept an app's functions. Ovi checked it on a Pixel 10 Pro running Android 17. It could not find an internal Android function it relies on, because newer Android versions changed that function. Another tool, Frida, could still hook apps the same way on that phone. Ovi therefore describes this as extra work for the kit's makers, not proof that Android 17 blocks the attack. The newest sample, dated July 29, 2026, still carried the old engine. He recovered samples built for Android 16 but did not report testing that version. He has not tested phones from Chinese makers. How It Takes Over a Telegram Account Inside a tampered Telegram app, the kit's code starts with the app and runs with the app's own identity and permissions, Ovi found. That gives it the same access as the signed-in app. Each tampered app also runs a local command server inside itself. The code for each target app is downloaded after installation, which makes the installer file harder to analyze on its own. Attackers can send any database query to the app's message store and get chat history back. Telegram's two-step verification (2FA) password is entered in the app, which uses it to generate a login proof on the phone. The kit hooks that step and copies the password in readable form before the app hashes it. With the password, the code can reset the account's logged-in sessions, change the linked phone number, or delete the account. Other parts of the code are designed to lock out the owner while keeping the attacker's session alive. The code can also hide the attacker's session from the device list that the tampered app shows the user. Doctor Web's description of Baohuo covers the same device-hiding. The backdoor also sends the account's phone number, name and password to its server every three minutes. Neither Ovi nor Doctor Web says whether a hidden session still appears on the user's other, untampered Telegram apps. Neither gives steps for securing an account taken over this way. Ovi says the code shows what the kit can do, not that attackers have used every step from start to finish. Earlier Android malware has also run legitimate apps with attacker code inside them. FjordPhantom did this to banking apps through virtualization in 2023, and so did the GodFather banking trojan in 2025. Ovi argues the kit is different because it is sold as a product. Customers can steer it remotely against any app its makers write a module for. The WeChat Part and the Leaked Back End For WeChat, the kit can also use app virtualization, running the unchanged app inside its own container, Ovi found. A command copies out the account's login identity. The app's data is then zipped and uploaded, and a bundled login script is used to clone the account. This part goes after the account itself, not its chat history. Ovi and another researcher, Jurre, also found the back-end code behind the kit on a self-hosted GitLab server. It was the one part of the setup not limited to approved IP addresses. The code shows a cloud console that merchants and resellers rent. Every command carries the customer's ID, so each customer aims its own share of the phone fleet at victims it picks. Commands go to phones in the kit's phone farm, a set of phones the operation controls, and to victims' phones. There, the kit captures login authorizations, adds friends in bulk, collects contact and profile data, and backs up whole accounts. A scheduler sets time windows, random daily limits, and per-account budgets, so the activity looks human and gets past the platforms' risk checks. The code calls this "account cultivation," in Ovi's translation. About three dozen developers, all working on China time, appear in the code's history, and some were still adding changes in October 2026. The leaked back end covers personal WeChat and WeCom accounts. Ovi says it did not appear to cover Telegram, and only one of several GitLab servers was exposed. Who Is Behind It Ovi ties parts of the operation to three companies in Hunan province, China. One is linked to the kit's brand website and a server certificate, another to a government website filing for a command server, and the third to the signature on the kit's Windows control program. He says a shared owner is "plausible, but remains unproven." The makers' own name for the product is YingGai, and the product line appears in records dating back to September 2021. The samples Ovi studied date from 2024 to July 2026. Ovi assumes the kit is used for financially motivated crime, given its focus on wallets and one-time passcodes. Doctor Web described Baohuo as "a tool for boosting the number of subscribers in Telegram channels." Indicators of Compromise The kit leaves two traces on a phone that Ovi calls reliable. One is a code file, TgJarPine.dex, in the assets of some tampered Telegram copies. The other is the original app copy that LSPatch, an off-the-shelf patching tool, leaves at cache/lspatch/origin/*.apk. Because that second trace comes from LSPatch itself, it can also appear in apps patched with the tool for other reasons. When The Hacker News checked DNS records on October 23, 2026, several of the kit's server and download domains no longer resolved. The domain for its version-upload server still pointed to 121.37.194[.]194. The kit's indicators include: SHA-256: 2fc4bad71eda25b9022ea7cb090d6419911ecd67e50e746b418f8a617a980301 (com.ucreator.tg, framework and command handlers) SHA-256: 0142749a159be3e41d28f910eebf28b577a282880bd0c2383bd7404189f4ff94 (com.uckj.tgx, loader) SHA-256: dcec9640271a782553599197bcb85367971a5bb4aa84c3787d1e49a3f4f9420e (org.thunderdog.challegram, tampered Telegram X, November 2024) SHA-256: 805834e6b8c12e180117a1816b48e387c33b53520f5a91cbf858441dc895e717 (org.telegram.messenger.web, tampered Telegram, July 2024) SHA-256: a90e3ab2b5cf306439a378faf7107a89196116ad7ee4ad5791c2ba8839ba21c4 (org.thunderdog.challegram, tampered Telegram X) SHA-256: f82ac2c525d1ed82e57b3f27ae689aeda46875a893ca4c42876b3166ba66bb20 (com.ucreator.va_vx, WeChat host) SHA-256: 99c5be579d218acfd2c7e2662528e7ad32a1a605d8efd1da732c13931bc30c4c (com.ucreator.va_yjb_client, Onion Box) SHA-256: 9c8b147f76312e651faabb1411a3270efca984dd8f33bd8ded3ea611c7c583a1 (uip.exe, Windows control program) Domain: hpncallback.gold5play[.]com (command server, not resolving on October 23) Domain: hpncallback.qianxunlbs[.]com (command server, not resolving on October 23) Domain: telegram-apk.uzyzx[.]com (download host, not resolving on October 23) Domain: hw.android.videoflow[.]cn (version uploads, pointing to 121.37.194[.]194 on October 23) IP: 159.138.237[.]10:32115 (Redis server) IP: 159.138.229[.]12:26379 (Redis server) Domain: r-bp1jehsclgbuu48m7tpd.redis.rds.aliyuncs[.]com:65531 (Redis server, WeChat part) IP: 43.225.141[.]209 (relay used by the Telegram part) URL: kfpt.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs[.]com/android/app/YingGai/ (hook downloads) Doctor Web has published its own indicators for Baohuo.

136bw3p.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a Microsoft 365 campaign that has been observed leveraging an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) relay to capture sign-in sessions and then replay the stolen tokens to break into email accounts at 79 organizations. Huntress, which observed the activity between July 14 and September 22, 2026, said it detected 497 successful Microsoft 365 sign-in events across the victim organizations from over 200,000 login attempts, with the attackers ultimately compromising 97 accounts and registering 48 rogue Entra devices. "Rather than guessing passwords, the attacker replayed sign-in tokens stolen from victims, and we've traced more than 200,000 failed login attempts from the campaign window back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range," Huntress researchers Andrea Hatcher, Susannah Matt, Matt Poto, and Andrew Schwartz said. The attack has been found to employ an AitM login page, which sits between the victims and legitimate Microsoft infrastructure to capture the entered credentials and MFA codes and relay the information to the real login page. The end goal is to collect the access token issued by Microsoft following the sign-in process so that it doesn't have to bypass MFA a second time. The "proof of login" token is subsequently replayed by the attacker from their own devices within minutes to conduct automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services. The approach has been codenamed token spraying, as it involves the attacker replaying many stolen tokens at scale across several organizations in a manner that's analogous to password spraying. Upon gaining successful access, the attackers moved to add their own authenticator app as a form of persistence to complete MFA challenges for new sign-ins and overcome scenarios where the stolen session token expires or gets revoked by the victim. In no less than 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were removed and a new method registered within three hours of the first sign-in. In one case observed on July 21, 2026, the threat actors activated a new authenticator app named "iPhone 13" less than 51 minutes after the session was hijacked. "Rogue devices served the same purpose," the researchers said. "The threat actor registered at least 48 fake computers in victim organizations' Microsoft directories. A registered device can give the attacker a more durable way to request tokens than the stolen session alone, and it stays in the directory until someone deletes it." Furthermore, the attackers have also been spotted setting up hidden email rules in victims' inboxes with names such as ".," "sss," "ss," "iT," ",.," "........," "s," and "d" to delete incoming mail with certain keywords referencing payroll, deposit, and bonus, or move them to obscure folders like RSS Feeds and Conversation History. In one compromised mailbox, the email rule marked all incoming messages as read and deleted them. The mailbox was then used to send outbound spam to hundreds of external recipients before Microsoft Entra ID Protection rated the account high risk. Huntress said the tokens originate from multiple sources, including AitM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process. The campaign was first observed from a Romanian IP address "193.26.115[.]221," which, according to VirusTotal, is used by a remote access trojan called AsyncRAT. The IP address is associated with a German hosting provider named 1337 Services GmbH. Data from GreyNoise currently lists 29 IP addresses matching the hosting provider, out of which 10 have been flagged as malicious and five are marked suspicious. Notably, the entity is linked to StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh, which allows paying customers to rent virtual servers. The domains linked to both StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh were taken down, alongside websites for Nulled, Cracked, and Sellix, as part of an international law enforcement operation dubbed Talent in January 2025. As of writing, the two platforms are operational, with the former now rebranded as exy[.]sh. "StarkRDP has always been operating by the law and is not involved in any of these alleged crimes, and the legal process will confirm this," the StarkRDP Telegram account said in a post dated January 30, according to independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs. "The only things that were seized is [sic] the website server and our domain. Unfortunately, no one can tell who took it and with whom we can talk about it. Therefore, we will restart operation soon, under a different name, to close the chapter [of] 'StarkRDP.'" Organizations who suspect a token replay compromise are recommended to revoke sessions and reset the password, audit Entra devices, review MFA methods, check for unexpected inbox rules or new enterprise applications, and restrict device-code workflow with Conditional Access policies. "Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented," Huntress researchers said. "Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally."

24ki3c.text: An automated campaign is using stolen GitHub tokens to plant workflows that print a repository's secrets into its GitHub Actions logs, which the attackers then download before deleting the runs. The attacks have succeeded in private repositories and GitHub Enterprise environments, according to an analysis by cloud security company Wiz. A GitHub safeguard that pauses suspicious workflow runs stopped every public-repository run Wiz checked, but it does not cover private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. Each workflow sits on a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters. Deleting a branch, or the run it started, does not undo the exposure. Every secret the repository could read should be rotated, and the token that pushed the branch revoked. Wiz has tracked the campaign since September 15 and calls it Gheist, after the user agent gheist that the attackers' tool sends with GitHub API requests. Wiz has recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, from personal projects to the private repositories of enterprise organizations. Wiz's analysis does not say how many organizations had secrets exposed. In private repositories and on GitHub Enterprise Server, GitHub audit logs show runs on the planted branches finishing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent. AWS CloudTrail logs show the organization's own workflows also running on those branches and assuming AWS roles, a sign that GitHub Actions ran there without approval. In enterprise organizations, the tool cycled through tokens from several users and automation accounts within minutes and cloned private repositories before planting the workflow. Hours later, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager. Wiz's analysis does not say where those credentials came from or who used them. As of October 24, the campaign was still running and changing. About two-thirds of the accounts involved were no longer available on GitHub. Wiz reported the activity to GitHub and says their disappearance likely reflects a response. Anyone with write access to a GitHub repository can read every secret configured in it, according to GitHub's documentation. A stolen token with that access is enough. For each repository a token can reach, the tool creates a ci-sync- branch and commits one file, .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, with the message ci: sync config. The commit is unsigned and includes the token owner's name; pushing it starts the workflow. The workflow prints the job's environment and every secret the job can read, encoded in base32. GitHub masks secrets in logs, but its documentation says this is not guaranteed once a value has been encoded or otherwise changed. Wiz says the base32 text no longer matches the original secret, so it prints in full. The workflow sets an empty permissions block. That limits the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, which the attackers do not need, and does not stop the job from reading secrets. One version of the tool also runs a job for each deployment environment in the repository, so secrets limited to those environments print too. These are often production credentials, according to Wiz. The tool then downloads the log through GitHub's API and deletes the run seconds later. Because the secrets leave through GitHub itself, there is no attacker server or outbound connection to block. Since July 28, GitHub has held workflow runs it identifies as potentially malicious until a collaborator with write access approves them. GitHub says the hold "currently applies to public repositories on github.com only" and that GitHub Enterprise Server does not have it at this time. Every public Gheist run Wiz checked, across all versions of the tool, was still waiting for approval, so its payload never ran. The hold only catches runs that GitHub flags. A new variant of GhostAction, a separate campaign, ran in public repositories until GitHub began blocking it on October 9, according to research from security company GitGuardian. Wiz says Gheist is distinct from GhostAction, which uses different workflow files. Around October 19, one version of the tool began pushing a second job meant for self-hosted runners, the machines organizations run themselves to process GitHub Actions jobs. It appears to target only repositories that have such a runner registered. The job is written to search the runner machine for credentials, including 31 types of tokens: private keys, process environments, AWS instance role credentials, runner credential files, and the Kubernetes service account token. Wiz describes the job as buggy, and its analysis reports no successful run. The sources Wiz could trace for the stolen tokens include infostealer logs and tokens exposed in earlier supply-chain attacks, such as the March compromise of the Trivy vulnerability scanner. Other attackers also use the same accounts. On October 6, 391 accounts, many of them also used by Gheist, renamed about 1,461 repositories to appear to be cracked software and spread malware. The renaming wiped 610 of the planted branches. Some victims also appear to be infected with PolinRider, malware that researchers have linked to North Korea. On October 19 and 20, three of them re-pushed their Gheist commits with a loader added to a vite.config.js file. Megalodon, a campaign that pushed secret-stealing workflows into thousands of GitHub repositories in May, had also hit 57 of the accounts. How to Check Your Repositories Wiz recommends these checks: Look for branches named ci-sync- followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message ci: sync config. In GitHub audit logs, look for workflow runs on ci-sync-* branches that were deleted within a minute of finishing, and for any activity from the user agent gheist. If your workflows sign in to a cloud provider with OIDC, check cloud audit logs for role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch. This works even if you do not collect GitHub logs. On self-hosted runners, look for the files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg and .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs. OIDC lets workflows sign in with short-lived tokens instead of stored cloud keys. By default, a token's subject includes the branch name only when the job does not use a deployment environment, according to GitHub's OIDC documentation. The published indicators are: User agent: gheist Branch: ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$ Commit message: ci: sync config, adding only .github/workflows/sync-check.yml String: toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120 String: ===== gdmp-pivot: File: .gdmp_pat File: .gdmp_patg File: .gdmp_sweep Git blob SHA (plain workflow): f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6 Git blob SHA (timeout version): d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291 Git blob SHA (separator version): 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4 Git blob SHA (self-hosted job version): c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d Versions of the workflow that list a repository's deployment environments vary by repository, so they have no fixed hash. What to Do If You Find a ci-sync Branch Wiz advises these steps for an affected repository: Rotate every repository, organization, and environment secret the repository could use. Revoke the tokens that pushed the commits, and check their owners' devices for infostealers. If a ci-sync branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the machine and its cloud instance role as compromised. Do not approve held sync-check runs, and do not run code from ci-sync branches. To make a stolen token less useful, Wiz also recommends these steps: Require reviewers on environments that hold production secrets. Limit OIDC trust policies to protected branches or environments. Use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens instead of personal access tokens. Run self-hosted runners as short-lived machines without Docker socket access or open access to cloud metadata. A job cannot read an environment's secrets until a required reviewer approves it, according to GitHub's documentation.

bsat5o.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 26, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Endpoint Security A malicious instruction file sitting in a developer's Downloads folder tried to make their AI coding agent install a known-malicious npm package, security firm Forever Security said in a report published last week. The company caught the attempt on a real customer's machine and stopped the agent before any code ran. It could not determine how the file got into the folder. The file was AGENTS.md, a plain-text instructions file that a coding agent, such as OpenAI's Codex, reads when it starts in a folder and follows as directions. It was dressed up as ordinary engineering notes. One section told the agent to add a server to its own configuration and install a package called function-color from npm. That package is part of a malware campaign that other researchers have documented separately: function-color pulls in a downloader called function-flag, which fetches and runs a Windows payload. Researchers at CloudSEK and Checkmarx, who analyzed the campaign, named it MALFEX. Two things, each harmless on its own, make this work, Forever said. An agent is built to trust and obey the instructions file in the folder it opens. And a web page can save a file to the Downloads folder on its own, without a click or a permission prompt, choosing the name and contents. Put together, a web page can drop a file the agent will treat as orders into a folder the agent trusts. Researchers did not establish that this is how the file was caught. To test whether the full path was possible, it built its own proof-of-concept page: visit it, and an AGENTS.md downloads silently into Downloads. Whether a real attacker used that route against the customer is not known. The firm then reproduced the attack on two coding agents to show that it was not specific to a single product. Against Codex, it ran the real attacker file inside an isolated virtual machine. The file, framed as routine project setup, told Codex to register a server in ~/.codex/config.toml and run a command that installed the package. Because that config file applies to every Codex session on the machine, the change would load the attacker's server in any folder afterward, not just Downloads. Codex ran the malware in more than 90% of attempts, Forever said. Against Claude Code, the working attack looked different and succeeded less often. A planted CLAUDE.md, framed as internal gateway setup, tried to make Claude write an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL into a project settings file, pointing its API traffic at a server Forever controlled. That one change leaks the session's login token, which is account takeover on its own, and lets the server reply as if it were the model and hand back commands the agent runs. Claude needs a person to approve a write like that and often refuses one that looks wrong; the long engineering-doc framing got the write approved about half the time, researchers said. There is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch, in Forever's view, because an agent following the instructions file in its folder is doing what it was built to do. The company compared it to a browser rendering a phishing page: the browser worked as designed, and the attack lies in the page. "There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch," Forever said. What to do Forever's advice is practical and needs no product: Do not start Codex, Claude Code, or any agent in ~/Downloads. It is the one folder the web can write to on its own. Look for instructions files you did not write. A stray AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, in Downloads or in a repository you just cloned, is the whole attack. Read it before you let an agent near it. Check the agent's own config. In ~/.codex/config.toml, watch for a server block or a changed base URL you did not add. In a project's .claude/settings.json, watch for an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or other API endpoint you did not set. Leave approval prompts and sandboxes on, and be wary of anything that tells the agent to switch them off. If you find a planted file, assume the login token leaked and rotate it. A stolen token is a live session, not just one caught request. In its own telemetry, Forever said that about half of its customers run a coding agent in their Downloads folder, and roughly a quarter of agent sessions open a browser. Those are the conditions the attack needs: an agent starts where the web can write, and, in many cases, an agent does the browsing itself, so no person is watching when a file arrives.

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. Integrate ANYRUN’s Sandbox in your SOC The post PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw Enabling One-Click File Account Takeover appeared first on Cyber Security News.

1aqcvsf.text: Every image scan returns hundreds of CVEs; the question is which ten your containers actually execute and which base image would zero the list entirely. We scored ten options with context and elimination weighted above raw detection. Evaluating scanners alongside the Top 10 Best Container Security Tools in 2026 reveals that static vulnerability counts alone do not prevent attackers who compromise container hosts through misconfigurations. Aqua’s Trivy takes 1 as the free floor everyone should run; Sysdig and Wiz complete a podium built on making findings mean something. Key Takeaways • 1 overall: Trivy the ubiquitous free scanner with platform depth above it. • Podium: Trivy (floor), Sysdig (in-use runtime filtering), Wiz (graph exposure ranking). • Strategy pick: Chainguard’s zero-CVE bases beat scanning by removing what scanners find. • One-vendor note: Grype and Syft are Anchore’s OSS pair SBOM-first scanning free. How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based: detection quality, SBOM support, context/prioritization, registry/workflow fit, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: context quality 30%, detection/SBOM 25%, workflow fit 20%, pricing accessibility 15%, elimination strategy 10%. The 2026 Container Image Scanning Power Rankings S.NO ToolAwardScore* 1Aqua (Trivy)Best free floor + platform9.1 2SysdigBest in-use prioritization8.9 3WizBest exposure-graph ranking8.8 4ChainguardBest eliminate-first strategy8.7 5SnykBest fix-oriented workflow8.6 6Anchore (Grype/Syft)Best SBOM-first OSS8.4 7JFrog XrayBest registry-native8.2 8Palo Alto (Prisma Cloud)Best CNAPP unity8.0 9Docker ScoutBest workflow-native7.9 10ClairBest OSS registry veteran7.6 *Editorial research-based scores, not lab results. 1. Aqua (Trivy) — Best Free Floor + Platform Aqua (Trivy) — Best Free Floor + Platform Snapshot: OSS free + Aqua tiers | Images, IaC, deps in one Why it earns 1: The most deployed scanner in the cloud-native ecosystem: fast, accurate, multi-target, and completely free with Aqua’s enterprise platform adding admission control and runtime security above it. Even as organizations maintain vigilance following threats like the Trivy supply chain attack on public registries, its multi-target engine remains the baseline floor no CI/CD pipeline should lack. Standout features: Image+IaC+SCA scanning; SBOM; CI-native; policy packs. Pros: Ubiquity; consolidation; free. Cons: Prioritization lives upstack. Bottom line: The scan without an excuse. 2. Sysdig — Best In-Use Prioritization Sysdig — Best In-Use Prioritization Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Runtime-informed filtering | Falco lineage Why it earns 2: Marking which vulnerable packages actually load into memory at runtime collapses CVE backlogs by 90-plus percent triage governed by execution truth rather than static theoretical risk. Built upon its open-source Falco heritage and Sysdig Threat Research on container escape vulnerabilities, it connects image vulnerabilities directly to live Kubernetes behavior. Standout features: In-use filtering; runtime detection; registry scanning; admission. Pros: Context that empties queues. Cons: Platform adoption. Bottom line: Only the vulnerabilities your containers run. 3. Wiz — Best Exposure-Graph Ranking Wiz — Best Exposure-Graph Ranking Snapshot: Platform quote | Agentless | Blast-radius context Why it earns 3: Image findings correlated with workload exposure, cloud entitlements, and network reachability determining which vulnerable container image actually endangers crown-jewel assets at cluster scale. Grounded in insights from Wiz threat research analyzing cloud attack paths, Wiz separates sandboxed images from workloads facing public ingress. Standout features: Graph correlation; agentless scanning; prioritization. Pros: Consequence ranking. Cons: Platform economics. Bottom line: The image ranked by what it can reach. 4. Chainguard — Best Eliminate-First Strategy Chainguard — Best Eliminate-First Strategy Snapshot: Published per-image | Zero-CVE minimal bases Why it earns 4: The strategic answer to alert fatigue: start with container bases that have nothing to flag. Minimal, continuously rebuilt, and cryptographically signed images resolve what CVE counts miss about container security by collapsing false positives and shrinking software bills of materials before deployment. Standout features: Hardened bases; provenance included; FIPS variants. Pros: Queue elimination. Cons: Migration engineering; per-image cost. Bottom line: The base with nothing to report. 5. Snyk — Best Fix-Oriented Workflow Snyk — Best Fix-Oriented Workflow Snapshot: Free tier + per-dev | Base-image upgrade advice Why it earns 5: “Switch to this tag, eliminate 80 CVEs” pragmatic recommendations that empty backlogs through direct action inside the workflows developers already use. Snyk pairs base-image intelligence with automated pull request remediation and fix advice so engineering teams can remediate Dockerfile bloat in a single click. Standout features: Upgrade advice; registry integrations; K8s monitoring. Pros: Actionability. Cons: Runtime context elsewhere. Bottom line: The recommendation that ships as a fix. 6. Anchore (Grype/Syft) — Best SBOM-First OSS Anchore (Grype/Syft) — Best SBOM-First OSS Snapshot: OSS free + enterprise | One vendor’s pair Why it earns 6: Syft generates the Software Bills of Materials the ecosystem standardized on; Grype scans them with precision free, accurate, and evidence-native, with Anchore Enterprise adding centralized policy gates. It provides the toolchain necessary for addressing what CVE counts miss about container security while pairing with container registry security tools to maintain artifact integrity across CI/CD environments. Standout features: Syft SBOM; Grype matching; policy (enterprise). Pros: SBOM depth; OSS credibility. Cons: Enterprise features gate up. oapp2e.text: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service that checks critical open-source repositories for security vulnerabilities and sends findings directly to project maintainers. The opt-in program uses the company’s strongest AI models to run repeated scans, giving developers a faster route to potential flaws without waiting for human review. According to Anthropic’s service overview, OSS Scanner builds on its work with Project Glasswing. The company says it had reviewed more than 6,000 vulnerability reports by October 2026 through its existing disclosure process. The new service offers a separate path for projects willing to assess AI-generated reports. Anthropic OSS Scanner According to the GitHub repository, the scanner first builds an enrolled project inside an isolated virtual machine with network access enabled. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. This extends Anthropic’s wider push into security research, including earlier work in which Claude uncovered 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. A Dockerfile must explain how to install dependencies and build the software. Developers can keep it in their own repository or beside project.yaml in the enrollment repository. Everything needed for building and testing must be downloaded during setup because the later audit cannot access the Internet. An optional threat_model.md file helps guide the scan. Maintainers can describe where untrusted input enters, which components are outside scope, and how they rate severity. They can also explain preferred report formats and patch requirements, reducing the need for the scanner to guess project-specific security expectations. Before applying, developers can use tools/validate.py to check their configuration and tools/check <name> to test the build. The checking tool runs with network access, so Anthropic warns users to test only trusted projects or use a separate machine. Configuration email addresses are public, making a dedicated security alias useful. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. Anthropic does not impose a 90-day disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings. However, a report later confirmed through its human-reviewed program may enter that disclosure process. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. Project owners still need to reproduce suspected flaws and test suggested fixes before treating them as confirmed vulnerabilities. Reports can be paused with disabled: true, while deleting the enrollment directory withdraws the project entirely Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. Which free scanner should we start with? Checkov (broadest IaC focus) or Trivy (one scanner across IaC/images/deps) both production-grade; consistency matters more than the pick. Terrascan serves Rego-first teams. What do paid platforms add over free scanners? Consequence ranking (which misconfig opens real attack paths), drift detection, fix automation, and governance workflow the difference between finding issues and closing them. How does IaC security prevent container and cluster compromises? Insecure templates often leave storage buckets open or configure cluster nodes without network isolation. Enforcing IaC checks ensures Kubernetes manifests and cloud infrastructure avoid misconfigurations that expose workloads, mitigating attack paths like malware compromising Kubernetes clusters through exposed services. Where do env0 and Spacelift fit? IaC automation platforms with policy-as-code guardrails security embedded in the deployment workflow, complementary to scanners, decisive for who-can-apply-what governance. What about infrastructure not in code? The blind spot: unmanaged resources escape IaC scanning entirely. Codification tools (Firefly) and cloud-posture platforms (Wiz/Tenable/Defender) close it. Verdict Wiz makes findings mean something, Snyk makes them fixable in-flow, and Checkov keeps the floor free for everyone scan at merge, govern at apply, and reconcile code against the cloud that actually exists. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement.
