6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. Teams planning automation can consult Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal access overview and API documentation and check their account limits. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. Weil$19,000,000Confirmed attack; ransom payment unverified. White & Case$30,000,000Not provided WilmerHale$17,000,000Confirmed May 2026 data breach. Total Reported$206,950,000 Silent Ransom Group, also tracked as Luna Moth and UNC3753, emerged after Conti shut down in 2022. Despite its ransomware label, it does not need to lock files. Operators trick employees into granting access, steal documents, and threaten to publish them. Law firms have been a major focus because they hold private client information. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. Smaller payments also reached regulated exchanges, creating potential leads through customer identity records. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. Employees should verify support requests through known internal channels before granting access. Organizations should restrict remote access, deploy phishing-resistant authentication, and train staff to recognize phone-based deception. Working systems don’t prove sensitive files stay safe. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. 150ej13.text: Multiple cybersecurity firms are reporting the successful exploitation of two recently announced PHP vulnerabilities, including one allegation of a breach involving U.S. government-affiliated servers. Cybersecurity firm GreyNoise said it has seen at least six successful exploitations of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, colloquially known as “PHP2Shell.” The bugs were added to a U.S. government catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this week, and federal agencies were given until Thursday to install patches. Another cybersecurity company, Dream, released a lengthy report detailing what it claims is a campaign by a Chinese threat actor involving the compromise of U.S. government-affiliated servers using the PHP2Shell exploit chained with another exploit of a large, unnamed vendor’s firewall software. Kfir Fleischer, Dream’s vice president of cyber research, told Recorded Future News that the attacker used PHP2Shell to execute commands on the firewall but it wasn’t enough to achieve full control, so they chained it with another vulnerability — CVE-2026-46300. The vulnerability, which affects Linux, was added to the same U.S. catalog of exploited bugs on Wednesday. “We recovered a custom PHP2Shell implementation tailored to the targeted firewall platform, version-specific profiles, exploitation logs and post-exploitation scripts,” Fleischer said. “The recovered logs record successful exploitation, including verification of root access by executing the id command through the installed webshell.” Dream did not specify the servers’ affiliation with the government. In total, the researchers found 24 compromised firewalls that gave the hacker the ability to extract credentials and enumerate directories. Most of the attacks took place between October 23 and 24. Fleischer said they are working with the firewall vendor and relevant authorities on investigating their findings. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) declined to comment on the report, directing Recorded Future News to previous advisories about PHP2Shell. Fleischer explained that they attributed the campaign to a Chinese actor due to the usage of Chinese language, known Chinese tools and Chinese AI models. Dream researchers found evidence that Claude code had been installed and that Chinese platforms like FOFA, DeepSeek and Kimi were used. FOFA, a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan, was used to identify about 19,000 internet-facing firewalls. Those were narrowed down to about 5,000 and then the attacker filtered it to find servers located in only the United States, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea. That was narrowed further based on exploit profiles, giving them a target list of 240 firewalls. Narrow targeting For 22 of the 24 firewalls attacked, the hackers did nothing beyond plant webshells that would allow later access. “While running mass exploitation on all targets related to the above geo-locations, which also had the relevant firewall version, they found 2 government-related servers among the breached firewalls, which they focused their efforts on, continuing a custom attack on those assets,” Fleischer explained. In the report, the researchers said the two servers were associated with one target and progressed beyond the initial stage. Both appeared to belong to a U.S. government-affiliated environment, they said. One of the firewalls that was attacked crashed and never came back online while the other was repeatedly targeted. The report said the PHP2Shell exploit chain was non-public and customized for the specific targets — something dozens of experts have said will be necessary for most exploitation of the PHP bugs. While the exploit follows the same underlying concept as others that have emerged, it “appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform,” they said. Once inside, the attacker “zeroed in on three specific servers in a U.S. government-affiliated environment.” Dream was unable to determine the full extent of the compromise but said the hackers likely have still-active, persistent remote access to the organization’s internal network as well as a complete organizational blueprint through the full Active Directory user and group listing. They also obtained account credentials, private keys and network topology that includes IP addresses and more. “If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure,” they said. Dream added that there was a “clear-cut focus” on government targets and the operation demonstrated a significant level of preparation and capability that set it apart from simple opportunistic exploitation. Expel cybersecurity expert Marcus Hutchins – who has been closely tracking PHP2Shell exploitation attempts — said the report appears to be tracking a Chinese threat actor known for targeting edge devices such as firewalls, routers, VPN appliances and more. He noted that the need to chain the PHP2Shell vulnerability with another kernel privilege escalation exploit was expected because it will allow the attacker to “go from unprivileged shell access to full root and kernel permissions, which enables them to do just about anything the device is capable of doing.” Several other experts said the campaign tracked by Dream represents more to the nature of how PHP2Shell will be used in the future. Viakoo’s John Gallagher warned that the same methodology of using scanning tools to find internet exposed operational technology systems using PHP2Shell could be used across many other types of devices beyond firewalls. “For any end-of-life devices using PHP2Shell, time is of the essence to get them replaced and off the network,” Gallagher said. 1jgil3x.text: General Motors on Thursday agreed to pay $220 million to settle a lawsuit filed by a coalition of 36 state attorneys general who alleged the company unlawfully sold consumers’ location and driving behavior data to outside parties, including data brokers. The data brokers then sold the sensitive data to insurers, affecting the prices drivers were charged for insurance, according to a press release from Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, who co-led the coalition’s efforts. In addition to the fine, the settlement requires GM to ask customers for their affirmative express consent prior to collecting or sharing consumer driving behavior and location data Beginning in 2016 and running through 2024, when the New York Times exposed the practice, GM allegedly enrolled millions of people in their “Smart Driver” program, allowing the auto giant to monitor their driving habits. The company allegedly marketed the program to customers by emphasizing participation could help drivers bolster their driving safety. The manufacturer also allegedly promised customers that it would not give insurers their data without their affirmative consent. However, GM allegedly broke that promise by selling the information to data brokers despite contract language it signed indicating the brokers planned to profit by providing the data to insurers. GM did not tell participating customers they would do so, the suit alleged. A GM spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the “agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices.” “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” they said. Pressure and deception Most customers agreed to participate in the Smart Driver program at dealerships as they were purchasing cars, and many have described pressure tactics that convinced them to sign. The one time sign-up process for drivers to enroll in Smart Driver also swept them into GM’s OnStar services. The data collection system operated with built-in factory surveillance far exceeding what insurers could collect by offering customers discounts to sign up for their own driving behavior trackers. Dealership employees were allegedly given bonuses for successfully enrolling customers in Smart Driver and dealerships also received incentives with GM ranking them against each other based on enrollment numbers, the press release said. The automaker also mistakenly informed more than 370,000 customers their data was not being monitored because they were not enrolled in Smart Driver, the attorneys general contend. GM subsequently unenrolled the drivers, but allegedly did so secretly and without alerting customers to the mistake. The data that had already been collected was allegedly not withdrawn from the data brokers and insurers. “The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific,” the press release said. “Insurers had data showing how many times a person drove their vehicle, the start and end times of each drive, how many times they braked or accelerated quickly, and whether they went faster than the speed limit.” Following an outcry prompted by the New York Times’ revelations, GM shut down the program. Under the settlement, GM must minimize the driving data it takes from consumers and safeguard their information as part of a comprehensive data privacy program, the press release said. The settlement terms are “significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct including by mandating internal and external data protection and privacy program assessments,” the press release said. GM also agreed to augment oversight and training for dealership employees to ensure they do not sign customers up for data collection programs without their approval. A similar lawsuit filed against GM by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2024 is ongoing. Paxton has alleged the car manufacturer handled drivers’ data in a “false, deceptive, and misleading” way by collecting data from customers, selling it to data brokers and allowing the brokers to in turn peddle it to insurers. Texas is seeking a jury trial and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per offense, along with a court order directing GM to delete the collected data. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1vjops2.text: Some attacks take real skill. Others just need someone to leave a door open. This week has both. Exposed passwords, old bugs still getting exploited, and trusted software doing things it shouldn't.There's a strange mix of clever tricks and careless mistakes. Hackers are borrowing trust from familiar apps, websites, and AI tools. Some are using AI to speed things up. Others are leaving their own attack files exposed. Not exactly careful work.Different stories, familiar weak spots. Here's what showed up this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. PHP2Shell attacks persist WordPress security company Wordefence said it's not aware of any WordPress site compromised through PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) as of October 28, 2026. "We continue to see PHP2Shell-related requests across the more than 5 million sites we protect," it said. "Those requests show ongoing scanning and exploitation attempts; they do not show whether an attempt succeeded. Our site-cleaning and incident response teams have not handled a WordPress compromise attributed to these vulnerabilities." 40,573 secrets exposed Hudson Rock's investigation into the FortiBleed credential harvesting campaign has uncovered 975 newly identified domains and 40,573 exposed secrets, including 37,076 local-user records and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records. The data comes from newly obtained 1,703 FortiGate source files associated with 1,689 host identifiers. "The configuration material dates to around February 2026, earlier than the likely May/June material examined in the first investigation," Hudson Rock said. The latest discovery has been codenamed FortiBleed 2.0. Institutional DNS hijacked Threat actors have used domain shadowing to place illegal gambling content beneath legitimate school and government domains in two unrelated operations. "In both cases, an unauthorized party appears to have gained access to DNS administration and created records that the original domain owners may not have noticed," Infoblox said. "Because the resulting hostnames sat within established institutional namespaces, they provided especially useful infrastructure for search-engine optimization (SEO) and traffic acquisition." One cluster, linked to a threat actor called Hidden Hawk, has been found to add individual CNAME records that mapped institutional hostnames to gambling pages hosted largely on Cloudflare Pages. The second campaign exploiting an Indian government domain "delegated entire subzones to third-party authoritative nameservers and used a wildcard, allowing many hostnames to be managed outside the victim's DNS environment." Put differently, the unauthorized DNS access creates new institutional hostnames, which resolve to infrastructure serving illegal gambling doorway pages. The pages also leverage the established reputation of school and government namespaces to ensure that the malicious URLs show up prominently in search engine results. AI banking credential warning Bank of America is reminding customers not to share banking credentials with AI agents. In an email blast to customers titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," the financial institution urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, "including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf." Android tightens contact access Google has announced that an upcoming Android release will no longer be able to directly write to contacts with the WRITE_CONTACTS permission. "Instead, you can use the standard contact intents (ACTION_INSERT, ACTION_EDIT, and ACTION_INSERT_OR_EDIT)," Google said. "Currently, if your app needs to save even one contact, you might be requesting WRITE_CONTACTS. But that permission grants broad access, allowing an app to make widespread changes to contacts across the device in the background, even without user interaction. Most apps don’t need such broad permission." 26,400 live credentials exposed A scan of 7.25 million public repositories on Gitee, China's largest indigenous Git hosting platform, has uncovered 26,400 unique verified-live credentials, including an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform and thousands of live cloud provider access keys, independent security researcher Ben Zimmermann said. Critical Fortinet fixes released Fortinet has released a "coordinated set of security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer" to address critical and high-severity flaws that were flagged using an AI-assisted vulnerability discovery approach. Details of the issues are being kept under wraps until November 10, 2026. With Fortinet devices becoming a favorite target for attackers, it's essential that users move quickly to apply the fixes. Zero-permission token theft Details have emerged about a now-patched flaw in Microsoft Authenticator (CVE-2026-80097 aka AuthMask) that could be exploited by installing and running a malicious application on an affected Android device and convincing the user to complete an authentication flow in the app by claiming to be a trusted app and getting the corresponding tokens. The flaw could be exploited to take over work accounts without requiring additional permissions. "Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to obtain authentication tokens and access resources as the affected user," Microsoft said. According to Enclave, "an unprivileged Android app with zero permissions could impersonate any installed Microsoft first-party app and have the Microsoft Authenticator broker hand it that app's tokens. The setup is a device with Authenticator installed and one work account signed into it." 32 fake AI bots hunt secrets Attackers are disguising themselves as AI agents to steal credentials. Cequence said it has tracked a single actor running AI agent impersonation at scale by posing as about 32 different AI bots, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, while searching for passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. "The malicious scanner runs from a major cloud provider and rotates through about 32 AI bot identities, spanning crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Perplexity, and others," Will Glazier said. "It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths. Each address sends a short burst of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds and then moves on. The scanner works through targets one at a time, around the clock, and first sends random nonsense paths to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique. It hit organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software, and stayed active from at least late September through late October." China-linked network intrusion The U.S. Embassy in Fiji has revealed that hackers linked to China broke into a regional organization based in Suva between July and August 2026. "Hackers with links to China maintained access to the organization's network over several days," it said. The embassy did not name the threat actor. Nor did it disclose what data the attackers may have accessed. Camera software weaponized Attackers have been breaking into enterprise networks via camera management software, according to new research from security firm Huntress, which observed multiple incidents in September and October 2026 and traced them back to a compromised application. Source code artifacts point to a Korean company selling analog and IP cameras and digital and network video recorders. The activity abuses the legitimate "WpcMon.exe" binary to sideload DLLs that establish outbound connections to a remote server. "This activity demonstrates how attackers can blend malicious code with trusted Windows components to evade detection," Huntress said. 68 GB government data breach In a major operational security blunder, an unknown threat actor stole 68 GB from a Philippine government agency, maintained a detailed log of the transfer, then left that log open on the internet at 13.163.205[.]35:80. "The copy finished in under 24 minutes on September 6, 2026," Hunt.io said. "The transfer log records 27 SQL Server backups whose filenames correspond to the case-management systems of a Philippine overseas-employment and migrant-worker administration. Beside the log sat the operator's toolkit, a rebranded GodPotato build, a PowerShell stager, two payloads and a full Impacket environment." AI model data exfiltration concerns Canadian AI company Cohere has claimed that it caught Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model unsuccessfully attempting to send data to China from its evaluation sandbox as part of a prompt instructing the LLM to detect malicious file download and execution by monitoring for curl processes downloading bash scripts to /tmp followed by bash execution. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," Cohere said. "We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training." Cohere has also released a dataset containing the model trace and corresponding raw token IDs in connection with the behavior. "The exact output is not guaranteed all the time, and many trials may be required to reproduce the behavior," Cohere said, adding "there are similarly unexpected URLs that the model also tends to output, most containing aliyunc." However, the findings have also led to social media chatter that the company is resorting to geopolitical fearmongering and that they are an attempt to clamp down on open-weights models. Post-quantum migration roadmap The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidelines that detail the timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. "The report describes different use cases and says why one migration might take longer than another," said NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who heads the PQC standardization project. "We understand there's not one strategy that fits all use cases, and we want to help people handle their migration while staying abreast of what's changing." AI-powered ransomware operation exposed SOCRadar has uncovered the live workspace (i.e., open directory) of a threat actor tied to the n0n ransomware group, which exposed the operation's full workflow as of September 2026. The directory at 185.157.161[.]148 includes an AI coding agent configured with about 150 models to produce hundreds of attack scripts, with more than $7,216 in usage costs. "Entry points included a credential stuffing campaign against 305 FortiGate SSL-VPN devices, exposed AWS keys, weak RDP/WinRM credentials, and compromised hosting management portals," SOCRadar said. At least 23 organizations across 14 countries are said to have been identified in the workspace, including a U.S. sports retailer, a cloud provider, a teachers’ union, a Venezuelan ISP, an Argentine ministry and a pharmaceutical subsidiary. Government AI access restricted The Swedish government has barred employees from accessing browser-based versions of ChatGPT or Claude on their work computers over security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data. "Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training," Euro News reported. 42 repositories hijacked JFrog and SafeDep have uncovered a campaign in which threat actors hijacked third-party 42 GitHub repositories across 11 owners to deploy payload blobs large enough "to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise." JFrog said, "The repositories contain execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, plus 12.9 to 13.7 MB polymorphic wrappers that all decode to the same hidden CI-publisher payload." The activity is assessed to be related to a Miasma-family npm worm propagated under various packages ending with "testmetest." According to SafeDep, the worm "shares code with Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' from June 2026 and adds the token-revocation wiper from Mini Shai-Hulud. The malicious versions steal credentials, spread to other packages and repositories, and install a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token." Unsuspecting developers who installed the packages had their data stolen and repositories compromised with malicious code to produce further malicious testmetest releases and run shellpanel workflows targeting cPanel systems through CVE-2026-41940, overlapping with a prior campaign detailed by Socket in July 2026. Android banking malware-as-a-service A new Android malware operation called MR ROBOT is targeting customers of Indian banks and transforming banking fraud into a subscription business, with cybercriminals renting customized banking trojans to steal OTPs, card details, UPI PINs and credentials while secretly forwarding calls to bypass security checks. "It is not a single-actor campaign but a rented crimeware platform: a master operator leases access to affiliates, who use a Telegram bot ('APK Shield) and a web control panel (v7.0) to build personalized banking trojans on demand and distribute them through fake Play-Store-style pages and messaging-app lures," CloudSEK said. The kit impersonates around 36 lure apps, including banks, utility providers, and government services. One affiliate is estimated to have intercepted 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices. MDM platforms abused for remote access Threat actors are abusing legitimate mobile device management (MDM) platforms, like Hexnode and Rippling, by using social engineering to enroll devices or install management agents, per Huntress. "Once established, MDM provides a trusted, privileged path for malicious activity, such as deploying rogue RMM tools and maintaining remote access," it said. Critical Gotenberg RCE exploited Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-42589 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical remote code execution flaw in Gotenberg, to deliver a Go-based reverse shell called "cache_base." The flaw was patched in May 2026. According to VulnCheck, the activity originated from a residential Japanese IP address in early October 2026. "The execution flow is straightforward: acquire a lock, collect host information, connect to C2, register the victim, and open a shell," VulnCheck said. Over the past 30 days, the vulnerability has recorded 1,358 exploitation events from 128 unique source IP addresses. Discord discussions go public Discord has announced it will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation, starting mid-December 2026. "Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you're looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord," it said. The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers and do not extend to private servers and direct messages. 800+ ransomware victims claimed The Gentlemen ransomware operation has claimed more than 800 victims across multiple regions and sectors, with most attacks targeting organizations in the U.S. and Europe. "The group supports multiple platforms, with ransomware variants targeting Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD systems, allowing its affiliates to target a broad range of enterprise environments," Acronis said. "The group's operations include the use of EDR-killing tools. In a recent incident, a custom dropper was observed deploying vulnerable Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver [CVE-2025-70795] and Lenovo BootRepair.sys drivers to terminate security processes." AI model loading RCE risk Pillar Security has disclosed an arbitrary-code-execution vulnerability in Unsloth's core model-loading path (CVE-2026-93348, CVSS score: 8.6). It has been fixed in unsloth_zoo 2026.8.14. "An attacker-controlled model configuration could cause Python code to execute during loading," researcher Ariel Fogel said. "The affected code ran inside the model-loading process, with access to whatever that process could read, modify, or authenticate to. In an AI development environment, that can include proprietary datasets, model artifacts, Hugging Face tokens, and cloud credentials. Exploitation required an affected loading path to process an attacker-controlled configuration." Unauthenticated root-level RCE XBOW said it identified an unauthenticated, critical-severity remote code execution bug in a public web application belonging to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC). "The vulnerable application was a resource/logistics calculator, not a voting machine or voter registration system," XBOW researcher Ariel Walter Garcia said. "The flaw allowed an unauthenticated attacker to execute code as root inside the backend container, with access to locally protected resources and outbound network connectivity, a privileged foothold reachable via a crafted unauthenticated web request." Session-hijacking RAT emerges A new remote access trojan called DarkCore comes with a dedicated browser that could let attackers access Gmail, WhatsApp, and MediaFire accounts using stolen sessions, while giving the impression that the activity is originating from the victim's own IP address. DarkCore was first advertised on cybercrime forums in August 2026. "The seller describes a browser that reuses those sessions to access work mailboxes, instant messaging apps, cloud storage and other services through the infected machine's IP address," BlackFog said. "The purpose is to make the access look like legitimate activity from the user." AI-powered malware framework Cisco Talos has disclosed details of a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework called NIK C2. The implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. "NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim's sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session," Talos said. "In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is an HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies." Three different versions of the malware have been identified to date since August 12, 2026. Talos said NIK C2 alters adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session. Malicious PDF delivers backdoor A phishing email using a FedEx tax invoice lure and containing a ZIP archive with a PDF has been observed triggering a multi-stage infection process to deliver a previously undocumented variant of the Sirius Backdoor. "The PDF abuses /OpenAction and /Launch objects to trigger an embedded Base64-encoded PowerShell command upon opening," Trellix said. "Execution relies on social engineering to trick the user into approving the PDF reader's security confirmation prompt. The PowerShell stager decrypts and reflectively loads a .NET assembly in memory. […]

38zuuh.text: A fake cryptocurrency trading app called Padre Terminal, previously available on the Apple App Store for iOS devices, has been linked to the theft of approximately $23,000 from 27 Solana wallets. Blockchain investigator Iris confirmed that one victim was compromised through the malicious App Store app, but has not determined how the other affected wallets were compromised. The researcher says the app drains wallets after unsuspecting users import their private keys into it. Padre was a cryptocurrency trading platform, mainly used to buy and sell meme coins on Solana. It was later renamed Terminal by pump.fun, a platform focused on creating, buying, and selling cryptocurrency “meme coins” on the Solana blockchain. Iris says the legitimate Padre trading service, now Terminal by pump.fun, is web-only, so any mobile apps impersonating it, including the one previously available on the App Store, are malicious. At the time of BleepingComputer's initial investigation, we found two Padre apps on the App Store (ID 6802739263 and ID 6717572591). The former was the Iris-confirmed drainer app, while the latter is likely pump.fun's official app, live since October 2024. The malicious crypto drainer app on the App Store Source: BleepingComputer The malicious Padre Terminal app has since been removed from the App Store, with its listing now returning a 404 error. Iris told BleepingComputer it suspects the trading interface of the fake app is served remotely, but has not directly observed the wallet-draining screen. According to Iris, the operation has drained 27 Solana wallets since October 25, 2026, stealing approximately $23,000 in cryptocurrency. The stolen cryptocurrency was traced to the Solana address 3LAgKYoNenWrGWT3U4XWhpgVJWyYkP9wKpiPk8TJT1LN. Iris says the attacker converted all remaining USDC (4,070 tokens) into SOL on October 29, eliminating the possibility of Circle freezing those funds. The attacker then transferred 192 SOL to a new wallet (H84yazsUVCF8eJ6brh27rURMHjdKEVv2BuLS4iuUUQbu). According to Iris, the two wallets held a combined 229.66 SOL, with no funds cashed out at the time of the researcher's update. The drainer remained active after the app's removal, with the latest reported theft occurring at 17:06 UTC on October 29. More suspicious apps on the App Store Iris identified at least five suspected crypto-brand impersonators on the App Store, including Padre Terminal, Axiom Pro: Focus, GMGN AI, HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools, and Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs. Their listings feature seemingly harmless descriptions, but user reviews below sometimes reveal their true nature, with many exposing them for wallet theft and scams. The Axiom Pro: Focus app, for example, had approximately 25 user reviews alleging wallet theft since February. One reviewer claimed the app had presented itself as a meme coin trading platform before changing into a focus application. A review of the GMGN AI app alleged that $2,000 had been stolen, while a review associated with HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools reported the theft of $2,020. Another app, Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs, presented itself as a notes application but had a review explicitly accusing it of stealing cryptocurrency. Two suspicious apps Iris discovered on the App Store Source: BleepingComputer.com Iris also found a script on the fake Axiom website containing backend addresses associated with Axiom, Aster, and GMGN impersonators, suggesting a common operator. However, Padre Terminal was not linked to that cluster. Also, a script on the GMGN website blocks visitors from several CIS countries, potentially indicating that the attackers are attempting to avoid targeting users in those regions. Iris has not independently confirmed cryptocurrency theft for the four suspicious apps. BleepingComputer has contacted Apple about the Padre drainer and the other four suspicious apps available on the App Store, but we have not heard back as of publication. In March 2024, a fake Leather cryptocurrency wallet app appeared on the Apple App Store, and multiple users reported losing their assets after connecting their wallets to it. Apple eventually removed the app two weeks later and blocked the publisher from its developer program. Users are recommended to follow links to the App Store from the projects' official websites and avoid installing apps with only a handful of downloads and reviews, or those published by entities with names that appear completely unrelated to the project. fj9ffk.text: A flaw in the Linux kernel's TCP code, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, affects Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), and other Linux distributions. The kernel's own CVE team rates it 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Anthropic said on October 27 that its AI model wrote an exploit that uses the flaw to let a remote attacker with no credentials run commands as root on Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener. As of October 29, Ubuntu and RHEL have not released a fixed kernel. Red Hat, Amazon, Oracle, and SUSE score the flaw between 5.9 and 8.1, lower than the kernel team's 9.8. The flaw is a race condition in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections. It can make the kernel read memory it has already freed, a bug type known as a use-after-free. The kernel fix credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge with reporting the bug. Neither the CVE record nor the fix mentions multipath TCP (MPTCP). The link between that feature and this bug comes from Anthropic's post. MPTCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. On Linux, an application must request MPTCP when it opens a socket. Anthropic's post says the flaw "was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches." For distribution users, that fix arrives only in the vendor's kernel package. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Amazon Linux have shipped fixed packages, at least for some of their kernels, but Ubuntu and RHEL have not. Which Distributions Have a Fix Distribution Vendor rating Status as of October 29 Fixed package or advisory Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, 26.04 LTS and 26.10 Priority High Work in progress None released Ubuntu 16.04, 18.04 and 20.04 Priority High Vulnerable None released RHEL 8, 9 and 10, OpenShift 4 Moderate, 5.9 (CVE page) Important, 8.1 ( advisory file) Fix deferred None released RHEL 7 Not applicable Not affected Not needed Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.18 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 24 kernel6.18-6.18.56-125.164.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3251) Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.12 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 29 in Amazon's advisory; Amazon's CVE page still says pending kernel6.12-6.12.113-138.209.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3335) Amazon Linux 2 Amazon Linux 2023, kernel package Important, 7.0 Pending fix None released Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9 and 10, UEK kernel Important, 8.1 Fixed October 16 ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, ELSA-2026-500399 Debian trixie (stable) No score listed Fixed October 16 linux 6.12.113-1 (DSA-6568-1) Debian 12 (bookworm) No score listed Fixed October 17 and October 22 linux 6.1.190-1 (DLA-4841-1) linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1 (DLA-4850-1) SUSE Linux Micro 6.2, openSUSE Leap 16.0 Important, 8.1 Fixed kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1 or later SLES 15 SP4 to SP6 LTSS, SLES 16.0, SLE Micro 5.3 to 5.5 Important, 8.1 In testing None released SLES 15 SP7 Important, 8.1 Affected, fix in progress None released Ubuntu also lists its cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernels as vulnerable or as work in progress. Red Hat says its fixes are "currently deferred to a future update." Neither Red Hat nor Ubuntu gives a release date. How the Bug Works The race happens during the TCP handshake. When a connection is completed, the kernel hands the IP options stored with the pending request to the new socket without copying them. If that socket is destroyed while another CPU is still using the options to answer a resent connection request, the kernel reads freed memory. IPv6 is not affected by this race because the kernel copies the options for IPv6 connections. The bug was introduced in Linux 4.4. Kernel developers applied a fix on October 5, ten days before the CVE was published. The fix makes the kernel wait until other CPUs finish reading the options before it frees them. Why the Scores Differ The kernel's CVE team added the 9.8 score to the CVE record on October 24, nine days after publishing the CVE. Its score assumes an attacker who sends a TCP connection request carrying IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options, then resends the request to try to win the race. The team rated attack complexity low, saying both sides of the race are "attacker-induced." In that case, the team says, the bug could send nearby kernel memory back to the attacker, corrupt kernel memory, or crash the system. As of October 28, the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) had not added its own score and showed the kernel team's 9.8. Ubuntu's page also shows that score. Red Hat's CVE page rates the flaw Moderate, scoring it 5.9 because the race is hard to win. It says the most likely result is a kernel crash, with memory corruption possible in theory, and that "no confidentiality or integrity impact has been demonstrated." Red Hat's machine-readable advisory file, updated on October 29, lists the impact as Important and scores the flaw 8.1, with high confidentiality and integrity impact. Red Hat's bug tracker changed the issue's severity from medium to high the same day. On that day, the CVE page showed Moderate and 5.9. Oracle and SUSE also score the flaw 8.1, with the same CVSS vector as Red Hat's advisory file. Those scores match the kernel team's on every metric except attack complexity, which the vendors rate high and the kernel team rates low. Amazon scores it 7.0. What Anthropic Says It Built Anthropic described the Linux exploit in an October 27 post about flaws that its AI model, Claude, found and exploited. The Hacker News covered the post on October 28. Claude wrote the exploit after "initial prompting," Anthropic said. The exploit works in two stages. First, the race makes the kernel send extra bytes back to the attacker. Once one of those replies contains a kernel address, the attacker can get around KASLR, the kernel's memory address randomization. Second, the same bug overflows a buffer and overwrites a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker had already placed in kernel memory. When the kernel calls that pointer, the payload executes a shell command of the attacker's choice as root. A lost race only fails that one connection attempt and does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep trying, the company said. In its test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes, and reaching command execution took 5 more minutes. The post does not include the exploit code, the kernel version, or the configuration Anthropic tested. Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach an exposed TCP service could trigger the race. Anthropic's root exploit, however, targeted servers with a multipath TCP listener. The post does not say whether servers without one can be taken over the same way. As of October 29, none of the vendor advisories, the CVE record, or Anthropic's post reports attacks using the flaw. It does not appear in a copy of CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog that Luxembourg's CIRCL last updated on October 28. What to Do Now Where your distribution has released a fixed kernel, install it. The table above lists the packages and advisories for Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux. If you build your own kernel, the fix is in Linux 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel's CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel. It says the kernel community does not support cherry-picking individual fixes. Ubuntu, RHEL and some Amazon Linux and SUSE releases have no fixed kernel to install yet. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its standards for being easy to deploy, suitable for most installations and stable. None of the other vendor advisories lists one. The advisories and Anthropic's post do not say whether turning off multipath TCP, or blocking incoming connection requests that carry IP options, would lower the risk.

jfx5l8.text: A newly identified advanced persistent threat (APT) group tracked as UAT-11473 was observed exploiting CVE-2026-20127, an authentication-bypass flaw in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers, to deploy a custom malware framework called KeyDrift. CVE-2026-20127 is a max-severity flaw that Cisco patched in February 2026, which allows remote attackers to gain privileged access to Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager and add rogue peers. UAT-8616 has exploited the vulnerability as a zero-day since at least 2023, and recent research also linked its exploitation to the Chinese Volt Typhoon state-sponsored hacking group. According to Cisco Talos researchers who reported on the activity, the UAT-11473 threat cluster appears to overlap with Volt Typhoon’s "Silent Train" covert access network, but they made no definitive links. In a report Lumen released yesterday, researchers revealed that the Silent Train framework allowed Volt Typhoon to evade detection while conducting zero-day vulnerability attacks. Deploying KeyDrift The attacks Cisco researchers observed targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research organizations, using the KeyDrift malware, which is a custom malware framework designed to operate on Cisco SD-WAN controller instances. "Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material," explained Cisco Talos. "KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records." KeyDrift has two primary components, PolyFlame and LittleFilch, for which Talos saw signs of ongoing development, including new anti-debugging mechanisms and varied process impersonation. PolyFlame runs inside legitimate vdaemon processes using modified service startup scripts and an injector for deployment. It supports command execution through a TinyShell-styled component, file uploads and downloads, and relaying communications between an attacker’s command-and-control (C2) server and multiple peers. LittleFilch is a control-session interception module that hooks SSL_read to inspect control-plane messages after they have been decrypted inside the controller. For predefined edge nodes, it extracts IP identifiers and a 32-byte field that Talos assesses to be AES-256 IPsec data-plane key material. It uses RSA encryption to protect the collected information, saves it to /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, and then transmits it over UDP to the attackers. Talos believes with high confidence that KeyDrift is designed to maintain persistent access to Cisco SD-WAN controllers, intercept control-plane traffic, extract cryptographic keys, and securely stage or exfiltrate the stolen data. Cisco recommends that system administrators apply the available security updates for CVE-2026-20127 and also consult the vendor’s dedicated hardening guide for Catalyst SD-WAN deployments.
